articles.content:
A tomatoey, southern Italian alternative to moules marinière – but who makes the definitive version?

A bundant, good value and ready in minutes, mussels are one of my favourite seafoods, but when it comes to preparing them, I rarely look farther than northern France. Italians, of course, also eat mussels, and this tomato-rich recipe is a particular favourite in the south – Neapolitans traditionally tuck into zuppa di cozze on Maundy Thursday but it’s found on menus all year round. With its bold flavours and oily, garlicky sauce, it’s a great alternative to creamy moules marinières , and similarly needs no accompaniment but a hunk of bread to make a meal, though chips, of course, are rarely unwelcome.

There’s not much to say about the main ingredient, except to bemoan the increasing difficulty in getting hold of live mussels due to the disappearance of so many fresh fish vendors, and the subsequent closure of supermarket fish counters (another rant for another day). Any remaining fishmongers should have British mussels, or they can easily be bought online . Don’t wash them until you’re ready to cook, when you should dump them in the sink and sort through them, discarding any with broken shells or that don’t close when you give them a sharp tap. Rinse with cold water; most mussels on the market are farmed, and rope-grown, so should be pretty clean, and I’ve never seen the point of scrubbing away at barnacles for hours when you’re not going to be eating the shells anyway (though please do enlighten me as to why I should bother). Remove any remaining trailing beards, though – I do have some standards!

The Silver Spoon dry-fries the mussels , then shells them to add to the soup later, while the Giallo Zafferano website steams them in garlicky oil and a little white wine, then removes them from the pot to be returned to the finished soup. It makes more sense to me to eat them as freshly cooked as possible – as Elizabeth David cautions in Italian Food, these “final operations must be carried out only immediately before serving”. Not only does this leave less chance of the shellfish overcooking, but necessarily ensures that every last drop of that delicious mussel liquor makes it into the sauce; tipping it back and forth, as in the Zafferano recipe, risks sacrificing a little, and when there’s not a lot to start with, that’s a gamble I’m not prepared to take.

Zafferano, whose recipe is specifically Neapolitan, includes octopus, squid and prawns alongside the mussels. Delicious as all those things are, we find the squid and prawns are overcooked and rubbery once they’ve been fried and then simmered in tomato sauce for 15 minutes. If you’d like to include them, I’d fry them briefly first, then return them to the pan right at the end (and buy the octopus ready-cooked, if you can).

David and the Silver Spoon are the only ones to use onions as the base of their dishes, with the former also including celery. More common is garlic in more or less generous amounts – Zafferano simply uses it to flavour the oil, while Marcella Hazan , perhaps reflecting the more Italian-American milieu in which she was writing The Essentials of Classic Italian Cuisine, sticks in a whole teaspoon and a half of the stuff, finely minced. I like the fiery flavour, especially alongside the chilli she also includes, plus this feels like a dish that should pack a punch.

And that also applies when it comes to the tomatoes. Hazan uses tinned, and reduces them to a jammy, oily sauce before adding the bivalves, a similar approach to David, but the latter’s more watery fresh fruit (and seeded summer san marzano plum tomatoes are about as far from watery as you’re likely to get) yields a lighter, fresher flavour. My favourites, however, are the cherry tomatoes suggested by Benedetta Rossi of the Fatto di Casa da Benedetta website, because they strike a good balance between the intensity of the tinned variety and the zingy acidity of plum tomatoes. My recipe uses a few more than Rossi’s, though, because we find her version a bit light on sauce, and cooks them for a little longer, in homage to Hazan.

The Silver Spoon flavours the base with saffron, Hazan chilli and parsley (Rossi adds the stalks, reserving the leaves as a garnish), and David suggests fresh marjoram, thyme or basil. I really like the echoes of Mediterranean French fish soups that the saffron brings with it, but my testers are ambivalent as to its merits, so I’ll leave that one up to you. Herbs, I think, are better used on top; not only do they look pretty against the glossy black shells and vivid sauce, but the peppery flavour of the parsley gets lost in the heat.

Not all recipes add extra liquid – the mussels give off enough to make a sauce, but it’s fairly scanty, so it makes sense to dilute it a little so everyone gets a decent spoonful alongside the shells. Wine is popular, used by David (who also adds a little water), Zafferano and Edinburgh’s Contini , while the Silver Spoon, whose recipe is more of a mussel soup garnished with a few actual bivalves than a pot of mussels, goes for fish stock. If you don’t drink, then this, with a spritz of lemon juice, is a decent substitute, but the zesty acidity of a crisp white is the ideal, not least because you can then drink it as an accompaniment.

Peppery parsley looks good, and tastes great, according to those who like it better than I do (if you share my aversion, you might like to experiment with mint, thyme or basil), and the garlicky toasts that pop up in the Silver Spoon, Hazan and Zafferano’s recipes are the perfect accompaniment, whether you want to spoon the mussels on top, so the bread soaks up their liquid, or serve it on the side to mop up the end of the sauce.

2 garlic cloves 500g cherry tomatoes 3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil , plus extra to serve 1 pinch dried chilli flakes (optional) 1 pinch saffron (optional) Salt 800g live mussels 2 tbsp white wine , or dry vermouth or fish stock 2 thick slices crusty bread 1 small bunch flat-leaf parsley , to serve

Finely chop one and a half cloves of garlic. Cut the tomatoes in half. Heat the oil on a medium flame in a saucepan large enough eventually to hold all the mussels, then fry the garlic and chilli, if using, until pale golden.

Stir in the tomatoes, saffron, if using, and a pinch of salt, then turn down the heat a little and cook until soft and pulpy. You can prepare the dish ahead up to this point if needed.

For this recipe, I’m assuming you’ve bought your mussels; should you have gathered them yourself, however, you’ll need to purge them in salt water overnight first, to get rid of any grit (have a look online for specific instructions ).

Either way, just before cooking, tip the mussels into a large colander and give them a good rinse with cold water. Sort through them, discarding any with broken shells or that don’t close when given a sharp tap (unless you can see the creature moving within). Scrub off any dirty patches (and barnacles, if you wish), and give any trailing beards (the weedy bits hanging out of the side of the shell) a sharp tug to pull them off.

Add the wine to the pan, turn up the heat, then tip in the mussels. Cover and leave to cook, shaking the pan occasionally, for five to eight minutes, until most of them have opened (discard any that do not).

Meanwhile, grill or toast the bread, then rub it with the remaining half-clove of raw garlic and drizzle with oil. Finely chop the parsley.

Divide the bread between serving bowls, then use a slotted spoon to scoop out the mussels and arrange on top (or serve the bread on the side). Bring the liquid back to a simmer, reduce slightly, taste for seasoning and ladle on top of the mussels. Sprinkle with parsley and devour immediately.

Zuppa di cozze – how do you like yours, and can anyone explain the many regional variations that surely exist on Italy’s extensive coastline? And which other mussel recipes would you recommend to anyone wanting an alternative to marinières?

articles.title: Modric ‘ashamed’ after 7-0 defeat by England; Republic of Ireland v Israel tensions build – matchday live
articles.summary: Latest news before Nations League fixtures Share your thoughts with us via email Harry Kane, now on 89 international goals from 124 games , says the Croatia performance has to be the blueprint for how England play. “Even when we were 1-0 up, we went for two, went for three, went for four, and that’s got to be our mentality. When you have a certain style of playing, you can’t just pick and choose when you want to do it. It’s just relentless. It’s non-stop. Celtic said the club would not be “intimidated or coerced by organised acts of disruption”, adding “there is a line between protest and deliberate disruption. Today that line was crossed … The club will protect its employees, directors, shareholders and supporters. The reputation of Celtic Football Club is non negotiable.” Continue reading...
articles.content:
On this day in 2003… a mighty comeback victory at Anfield for Arsenal’s soon-to-be-Invincibles.

It’s probably fair to say not everybody loves Jesse Marsch , but I’m sure we can all agree* he’s a great talker. Here he is in conversation with Joe Callaghan.

* May not actually be sure we can all agree, this being the year 2026 and that.

Andy Robertson isn’t quite the elemental force of a few years ago , when he was one of the best left-backs in the world, but he is still going strong and last night he was his 100th cap for Scotland.

It feels unbelievable. To hit the 100 mark is pretty special. It’s something that I feel as if I’ve been chasing forever. But since became close, I then really wanted to just get it over the line. A hundred caps for your country is incredible. Not many people get to achieve that and I know how lucky I am to be able to be one of the ones to do that.

Robertson is on course to overtake Kenny Dalglish as Scotland’s most-capped player by the end of year. Dalglish played 102 times for his country.

Hopefully I can [overtake Dalglish] because I want to keep playing and I want to be in a Scotland jersey for years to come, which obviously results in me hopefully taking over Kenny. But I’m only the second male player to get to 100 caps and I have to enjoy that. I think us footballers are a bit guilty of not enjoying it and not realising sometimes what you’ve achieved, so I’ve made a conscious effort to try to do that.

I know what I’ve achieved for me and my family and it was a really special night for us. I’ve had lots of messages, more than normal. A lot of ex-players, a lot of managers, a lot of family members and things like that, so it’s been pretty nice to be on the phone, and I’ll start getting back to them slowly but surely.

Plenty more Nations League action today. These are the fixtures, all 7.45pm BST kick-offs unless otherwise stated.

John Stedman writes in with another on this day from 1989 : Southend United 3-2 Tottenham Hotspur in the League Cup (3-3 agg; Spurs go through on the away goals rule).

“A plausibly - and pleasingly - contemporary scoreline,” says John. “Were Spurs not already out of the League Cup, of course. Schadenfreude is a dish best eaten very cold.”

So … can we play another World Cup, then? Can we just undo and rewind? Forget whatever it was you thought you saw in Atlanta . We’re actually ready now.

Although not, repeat not, if any part of this involves playing football in front of 6,000 excitable children, the combined effect of which was to create an atmosphere in Rijeka the adult human ear is simply not designed to process.

This was a dreamlike occasion on many levels, from its quietly farcical staging, to a relentlessly high-grade England performance and a deserved 7-0 win, all of it glossed in the moment by the striking beauty of the setting.

Rijeka is a gently crumbling Italianate coastal town, the stadium lodged up in the hills facing into the blue of the Adriatic. From the stands here you could switch between watching Jude Bellingham cruise about the pitch like a human superyacht to following the cargo ships crawling across the curve of the bay, the grey-green fade of the hills below, white towers by the shore, like a pocket-sized Balkan Rio de Janeiro.

On this day in 1997… Dennis Bergkamp provides further evidence that Arsene Wenger’s Arsenal are the real deal .

“Even the most bigoted football fan would not speak ill of Luka Modric,” writes Krishnamoorthy V. “What a treasure. Not one controversy, not one ‘I am bigger than the game or the team’ moment, a commitment that borders on surreal, a work output that would put an 18-year-old to shame. A true role model if there ever was one. Relax, Luka, everyone has an off day. Ask Brazil, Real Madrid, Man Utd and Aston Villa.”

Sassuolo forward Kieron Bowie was full of the joys after scoring his first goal for Scotland in their 2-0 win against North Macedonia. Bowie’s goal set up Scotland’s first victory under Sebastien Pocognoli.

The manager’s put a lot of trust in me to start the last two games. It’s a fresh start for me with a new coach and different ideas. He said to me, ‘You don’t need to prove yourself, just go and do what I know you can do’, and I feel like I’m doing that.

In terms of the meaning for me and for Scotland, and for the coach, it’s the first goal for him and our first win, so I think that tops the lot.

It’s been a very good international window for Bowie, who was left out of Steve Clarke’s World Cup squad but now appears to be a regular starter.

Obviously I was disappointed. I felt like I’d done as much as I could. I moved to Serie A, I scored goals for a struggling Verona team and that was as much as I could do so I was happy with where I was at and how I’d played. But these things happen, you’ve just got to bounce back, and I feel like I’m doing that.

I think people, obviously Scottish fans, have an idea of how I was when I was at Hibs, and that’s all they can remember. But I feel like since I moved to Serie A, it’s a different challenge against more experienced players and at a higher level, so I feel like I’ve definitely kicked into another gear, and I feel like I’m showing that.

If you prefer live actual sport to live sports news, we have a couple of pieces of F5able goodness for you.

We’ll be launching our Next Generation 2026 feature next week . In the meantime, why not check in on the class of 2025? Here’s our October 2026 update on Bayern Munich’s Lennart Karl.

Already a superstar after playing a big part in Bayern’s double in 2025-26 and hopes were high that he would make a big impact at the World Cup, but Karl suffered a torn muscle in his left thigh on the eve of the tournament. “It hurts incredibly to miss the biggest tournament,” Karl wrote in an Instagram post. “Unfortunately, injuries often come at the worst possible time.”

Thanks John, morning everyone. Let’s start this mini-session with Thomas Tuchel’s comments on Bournemouth Alex Scott, who made an outstanding full debut against Croatia.

First start and what a start, what a performance. He is so smooth on the ball, his decision making is at the highest level. He plays with so much confidence. He is so active, so confident. The work rate off the ball. He is just the complete package. He gave us a lot of mobility and a lot of variety and work rate in the centre of the pitch.

Tuchel was also understandably effusive in his praise of England’s attacking quartet of Bukayo Saka, Jude Bellingham, Harry Kane and Anthony Gordon (with help from Morgan Rogers). After a 7-0 win, it’d be a bit rum if he called them out.

The movements in the last line are at the highest level and are getting better and better. That’s why I didn’t want to change so much from match to match, to get the fluidity going and to get the movements going and to get the automations right within the front four.

They are very good together at the moment and they enjoy playing together. These are complete performances. It’s a team effort but the front four look very dangerous.

They just want to play like this. It’s their belief and it’s also their wish and conviction to play like this. So this is not something that we have to convince them to do. It’s just the way they want to play.

Talking of 7-0 wins, Argentina beat Burkina Faso by that very same scoreline, as they prepared for the big Messi send-off against Benin.

Lautaro Martínez, Gianluca Prestianni, Nico Paz, Julián Álvarez, Franco Mastantuono, Giuliano Simeone and an own goal by Moumoune Diallo got the goals. The visitors to Buenos Aires. Burkina Faso’s squad arrived in Buenos Aires just five hours before kickoff after a flight from Morocco was cancelled. Several senior players had already declined to travel.

Slaven Bilic, the Croatia coach, also had his say, speaking to Jutanrji, the Croat newspaper : ““It is difficult to say anything after a night like this. We are sad, disappointed, and I feel sorry for the fans and the children who were at the game.

“We talked, it is hardest for us, and we did not expect this could happen. I don’t know what to call it, whether it’s a blackout, but it’s hard to analyse a game when you lose 7-0. We knew they were a top team, but that we couldn’t match them in any part... that then attacks your confidence, your will, everything falls apart and goes the wrong way.

“I said this to myself and to everyone, I don’t believe that England would beat Estonia 7-0 at this moment. That is unforgivable for us. We can get out of this with a good performance against Spain, there is time for that. Now is the right time to show unity and character. I’m talking nonsense saying we will beat Spain, but we need to show a brave and good Croatia. We need to show heart.”

The veteran spoke after the 7-0 Nations League defeat: “It is difficult to find an explanation for such ⁠a performance without duels, fouls, aggressiveness, togetherness... I’ve been here ​for 20 years, but ‌for the first ‌time I feel ashamed after a game.

“You ‌can lose, or play against an opponent who is better - and they are right now. But in any case, losing like this and squandering the reputation we’ve built over the years is unacceptable.

“You can’t play football like that. ‌You can’t play with two players less, you can’t play like this, and we looked like ​we had 4-5 players less. A catastrophic night.

“We ​need to ​pull ourselves together, stay together ​because a new difficult game awaits us. And we ‌have to ​show our ​true colours, that there is defiance and pride in us, desire, willingness, togetherness, these things cannot be lost overnight.“

A second meeting of the Republic of Ireland and Israel was preceded by further stormy scenes in the press conference.

One reporter questioned Hallgrímsson on his thoughts about the incident on Wednesday during a Flydubai flight from the UAE to Israel .

“What do you say about the people that you support? Their ideology is based on murder,” the journalist asked. “Just this week, one of them tried to kill 170 Israeli passengers, including 27 innocent children and thousands of others.” An Irish press officer replied: “We are not doing any questions like this today. We are doing football questions.”

Another journalist then addressed the Ireland manager: “Your players call our players monkeys during the match …”, only to be immediately interrupted by an FAI official repeatedly insisting “that is completely untrue”, while the microphone was taken away from the reporter.

Saudi Arabia is quietly shelving plans to build one of its most ambitious stadiums for the 2034 FIFA World Cup, two sources familiar with the matter said, after delays ⁠and downscaling of the futuristic development ⁠housing it.

The Neom Stadium was ​billed as an elevated arena in a glitzy 100-mile (160-km) steel and glass structure known as The Line, in turn part of the broader development known as Neom.

Neom was introduced about a decade ago as a centrepiece of de ⁠facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s Vision 2030, an ambitious plan to diversify the economy and cut reliance on oil. Yasir Al-Rumayyan, governor of Neom’s owner the Public Investment Fund, confirmed in April that The Line was no longer a priority, and said ⁠it was not vital before 2030, the original delivery target for its first phase. He denied any projects had been cancelled.

However, according to two sources, plans to build ​the Neom Stadium have now been shelved indefinitely.

Sébastien Pocognoli got his first win as Scotland manager. Will Kieron Bowie’s goal be the beginning of golden years?

John McGinn’s 22nd goal for his country, coming from the penalty spot, meant the scoreline at least almost reflected Scotland’s dominance. Only Scott McKenna’s late sending off and a failure to notch three, four or five could have irked Pocognoli. Scotland remain alive and kicking in section B1 of the Nations League while aware they will face far, far stiffer challenges. Scotland needed to be professional in North Macedonia and met that task appropriately.

South Korea’s Asian Games football captain , Lee Gi-hyuk, has apologised for boasting that his gold medal meant he did not have to do military service, report AFP.

South Korea defeated hosts Japan 1-0 on Saturday in the men’s final. Afterwards, Lee smiled as he held up his gold medal to reporters and said: “I’m not going to the military.” Able-bodied South Korean males are usually required to perform between 18 months and two years of military service before the age of 28. But the government rewards Asian Games gold medals and Olympic medals of any colour with an exemption, meaning they will carry out just weeks of light basic training instead.

The 26-year-old Lee, a defender who plays in the domestic K League, apologised for “the thoughtless remarks I made and the way I behaved after the match, things I should not have said or done, both as captain and as a player”. In a statement on Instagram he said he was “caught up in the happiness, adrenaline and excitement of the moment”.

“I am deeply sorry to the fans who are currently fulfilling their military duty, as well as to all those who sincerely supported us. As an adult I should have thought carefully before speaking. I deeply regret having spoken so carelessly, and I will continue to reflect on my actions. I sincerely apologise to all the fans who have supported us wholeheartedly and who are doing their utmost to fulfil their military duty.”

A hundred caps for your country is incredible. Not many people get to achieve that and I know how lucky I am to be able to be one of the ones to do that.
Robertson is on course to overtake Kenny Dalglish as Scotland’s most-capped player by the end of year. Dalglish played 102 times for his country.

Hopefully I can [overtake Dalglish] because I want to keep playing and I want to be in a Scotland jersey for years to come, which obviously results in me hopefully taking over Kenny. But I’m only the second male player to get to 100 caps and I have to enjoy that. I think us footballers are a bit guilty of not enjoying it and not realising sometimes what you’ve achieved, so I’ve made a conscious effort to try to do that.

articles.title: Gallant Knights’ NRL grand final loss ‘hurts so much’, says standout Kalyn Ponga
articles.summary: Newcastle fullback was brilliant in 19-18 loss to Sydney Roosters Ponga pays tribute to fans who packed into Accor Stadium The emotion of the week finally took its toll on Kalyn Ponga, who starred for Newcastle despite their 19-18 defeat to the Sydney Roosters in the NRL grand final. The Knights fullback was responsible for many of the match’s most dazzling moments – a constant menace with ball in hand on both sides of the field. He saved a four-pointer when pressuring Mark Nawaqanitawase’s aerial put-down in the first half. He ran away for a length-of-the-field try, the undoubted highlight of a thrilling encounter. The pink headgear was impossible to miss. Continue reading...
articles.content:
The emotion of the week finally caught up with Kalyn Ponga, who starred for Newcastle despite their 19-18 defeat to the Sydney Roosters in the NRL grand final.

The Knights fullback was responsible for many of the match’s most dazzling moments – a constant menace with ball in hand on both sides of the field. He saved a four-pointer when pressuring Mark Nawaqanitawase’s aerial put-down in the first half. He ran away for a length-of-the-field try, the undoubted highlight of a thrilling encounter. The pink headgear was impossible to miss.

Despite his brilliance, however, the Roosters proved too clinical and overpowered the gallant Knights in the second half. The result came at the end of a week the city of Newcastle experienced incredible highs, but – with Saturday’s accident in Wallsend and Sunday’s defeat – it was not without lows. The massive support for Newcastle at Accor Stadium on Sunday only amplified the sentiments.

Ponga was exhausted at the end of 80 minutes, physically and emotionally. “It hurts so much,” the Knights captain said after the match, his voice wavering. “I know we did them proud, but the ultimate goal is to win a comp. [I] can’t thank them enough for their support. We’ll be back.”

Most of the 80,814 in attendance were backing the Knights, and the stadium roared as the Novocastrians raced to a 12-0 lead. The relentless Roosters stayed patient and pegged them back, and led by seven late in a match in which they enjoyed 57% of possession.

Newcastle found a way back, however, scoring a late try to give them one last shot. Despite the urging of their fans, they could not conjure one more of their trademark long-range tries.

Ponga said he was “super proud” of the team, despite the result. “Wooden spoon last year, if you had have said we were playing in the grand final [at the start of the season], I would have said you were kidding,” he said.

Speaking to press afterwards, he was composed and reflective about what had been an extraordinary week for Newcastle. “I’m so grateful for this week to see the spirit, pride of our community, the connection that it’s brought to so many people,” he said.

“Newcastle people are tough and they’ve had to do it tough yesterday with something that happened and our thoughts with those people as well – the tragedy that happened as we were leaving – but our community just really rally around each other.

“Nothing this week was a burden on us. Someone said before the game was it distracting? Fortunately we get to be in this position, we get to experience what we experienced this week, and it’s definitely a feeling I’ll chase again.”

Roosters captain James Tedesco was full of praise for his opposing fullback, who has finally entered the conversation this year as the best player in rugby league.

“If you stop Kalyn, [you go] a long way to winning the game,” Tedesco said. “Our boys on the edge did a great job defending him. I mean, they just keep asking questions, he’s so hard to handle, our boys did a great job.”

Knights coach Justin Holbrook said there is no player in the competition he would like in his team more than his captain. “I just love everything about him, I just love the way he leads our team, [he’s] so infectious. I said to him a few times this year, if we’re going to get to the end of the year and give it a shot, he’s going to have to be our best player,” he said.

The coach agreed that the team relished the week. “I got asked that many times, is it overwhelming? Is it overwhelming? It was never overwhelming, and we didn’t even care what we had to do, we were just going to be ready to go.”

articles.summary: Updates on the big race in Paris (3.05pm), news and more Get in touch! Send your thoughts to Greg here 1.09pm Qatar Prix Jean-Luc Lagardere betting Folsom Blues - 11/10 Avec Toi - 3/1 Amusingly - 6/1 Mans Best Friend - 15/2 Florida Bay - 16/1 Imperial Strike - 16/1 Alfred Wallace - 30/1 Aix La Chapelle - 40/1 50/1 BAR Race odds provided by Oddschecker Continue reading...
articles.content:
1.09pm Qatar Prix Jean-Luc Lagardere And they’re off for this key race for juveniles … Crusherman leads in the early stages but

Social media reports suggest that Spirit Tango, who ran in the first race at ParisLongchamp today, has had to be put down. A very sad postscript to the Prix Marcel Boussac and news which follows the death of another horse on Arc weekend after the demise of another British runner in Fallen Angel on Saturday.

Green Empress provided trainer Joseph O’Brien with another big-race success in a stellar year when narrowly holding off Data to win the Prix Marcel Boussac, the forst race at ParisLongchamp on Arc day.

O’Brien said: “It’s really special for us to have a Group One winner on this day and she has been progressive – she’s only ever been beaten by Sun Goddess all year. She has a super pedigree, being by Saxon Warrior out of a Sea The Stars mare. We see her as a miler that might go 10 furlongs at some stage.

“We’ll see how she comes out of today and discuss with the owners whether she’ll go to America [for the Breeders’ Cup] or whether we wait for next year.”

O’Brien added: “We’re very lucky to have the support of some great people and a wide variety of owners. For us it’s about performing and executing at big meetings. It’s fantastic to have a big winner on Arc day.”

1.09pm Qatar Prix Jean-Luc Lagardere preview The second two-year-old race on the card is often assumed to be the colts’ version of the Boussac, but it’s over seven furlongs rather than a mile and while the great majority of the field are colts, fillies are also eligible and Francis-Henri Graffard’s Amusingly is an interesting contender with the 4lb sex allowance at the bottom of the card. Aidan O’Brien’s Happily, in 2017, is the only filly to actually win this century, though, and as was the case in the opener, it is Joseph O’Brien, and not his father, who fields the likely favourite in Folsom Blues.

The son of Blue Point bolted up in the Group One National Stakes at the Curragh three weeks ago, finishing six lengths clear without being asked for maximum effort, and though a draw in stall 10 is not ideal, a repeat of that will make him hard to beat. That said, Folsom Blues has been beaten in three of his five starts to date, unlike Avec Toi, the likely second-favourite, who arrives with a perfect 4-from-4 record. He is stepping up from Group Three company but clearly brings considerable talent to the fray, though I’ll be more than happy to back Folsom Blues to beat him, not least because his latest rout was backed up by a strong time.

12.31pm Qatar Prix Marcel Boussac And they’re off for the opener on Arc day … Nevermindtherain is slowly away and Green Empress the favourite is in midfield … Spirit Tango leads at halfway … So Lovely is right there as they turn for home … Green Empress now delivers her challenge and will just hold on a very strong challenge from Data. sadly, Spirit Tango appeared to suffer a very bad injury during the race.

A dozen runners for the Arc meeting’s premier event for juvenile fillies, won last year by an Arc contender, Diamond Necklace. It’s a race where the visitors have enjoyed plenty of success in recent years but the home team have also managed to hold their own, with 10 wins for French stables in the last 20 years and the remainder shared between Ireland and Britain. Aidan O’Brien, needless to say, is the most successful raider from across the water, with six wins since 2005, but it is his son, Joseph, who fields the likely favourite in Green Empress, the runner-up behind his dad’s hugely impressive Sun Goddess in the Moyglare Stud Stakes last time.

She sets the standard, but she was also six-and-a-half lengths adrift and rivals like Christophe Ferland’s Allela, who looks the pick of the locals, must be taken seriously. She is stepping straight into Group One company after winning a couple of minor events at Deauville and Chantilly but is still just 1lb behind Green Empress on Timeform’s ratings with two fewer races in the book. Her stable-companion, Data, is another to consider having run third in a Group Two last time. O’Brien snr fields three runners with Ibelieveicanfly (Ryan Moore) looking like the first-string but all three have something to find on ratings, while Miss Miniver , beaten less than a length-and-a-half when fourth in the Rockfel at Newmarket nine days, is an interesting runner in Godolphin blue from the Roger Varian stable.

Here’s the line up (and what a tasty one it is ) for today’s action at Longhamp 12.31pm Qatar Prix Marcel Boussac SKY 1.09pm Qatar Prix Jean-Luc Lagardere SKY/ITV 1.47pm Prix de l’Abbaye de Longchamp Longines SKY/ITV 2.25pm Qatar Arabian World Cup SKY/ITV 3.05pm Qatar Prix de l’Arc de Triomphe SKY/ITV 3.50pm Prix de l’Opera Longines SKY 4.25pm Qatar Prix de la Foret SKY We’ll be giving you Greg’s previews and the betting about half an hour before each race.

Bienvenue à Longchamp on one of the most eagerly anticipated days of the racing year: the Prix de l’Arc de Triomphe, the most valuable and prestigious race of the European season, is due off at 16.05 local time (1.05pm BST) and in all there are half a dozen Group One events on the card in the Bois de Boulogne on the busiest afternoon of top-level racing in Europe all year.

The Arc needs little introduction: it’s roll of honour speaks for itself. Ribot , Sea-Bird , Mill Reef, Dancing Brave , Peintre Celebre and Sea The Stars all have their names up there in lights, and that’s to name but six.

If you’re going to click on one of those links, I’d recommend Sea-Bird for several reasons. You can’t beat a Peter O’Sullevan commentary for one, and it’s weird to see the field completely disappear from view for several seconds behind the trees in the middle of the track (the coverage cuts to a bemused Frenchman in the stands). But above all it’s for the way he bursts clear at the top of the straight, putting the race to bed with an effortless, ground-eating stride that looks as though he’s running on his own personal conveyor belt.

The Classics sort out the best horses of every generation, but the Arc sifts the all-time greats from the best of several generations could see Daryz join the very small band of colts that have won the Arc in successive years. Last year’s winner has drawn well in stall five, but now gives weight to a strong cohort of three-year-olds including Thundering On, the Oaks winner; Maltese Cross, the Grand Prix de Paris winner; and his stable-companion, Varandir, who took one of the key Arc trials, the Prix Niel, last month.

Among the older horses, Kalpana, the King George winner, has improved again this year at the age of five and bids to set the seal on Andrew Balding’s best-ever season. And Minnie Hauk, last year’s narrow runner-up, will be a major player if she can bounce back to that form.

The going in Paris is unusually quick for the time of year, which is good news for some contenders – including Maltese Cross and Kalpana – and perhaps less so for Thundering On. But as the field turns for home and starts to fan out across the wide expanse of Longchamp’s final straight, the question will be the same as ever: which horse will rise to the challenge and stamp its name in Arc history?

We’re underway at Longchamp at 12.31pm BST with the Prix Marcel Boussac for juvenile fillies and there is more than an hour to build up to the big race after the Prix de l’Abbaye at 1.47, so kick back, relax and let the Guardian’s live blog pilot you through one of the best afternoons of the racing year.

articles.content:
As he prepares to face his home nation, the Canada manager reflects on his adopted country’s soccer, its prime minister, and its place in the world

Peak leaf hasn’t yet arrived in Montreal but the bursts of gold and butterscotch up on the hill that gave this place its name still mushroom out by the hour.

Sitting in a glass-panelled hotel mezzanine at the foot of Mount Royal, Canada men’s coach Jesse Marsch has his mind on another harvest. When this extended autumnal international window ends he will decamp to Italy, where the olive crops at his Tuscan villa are ready for reaping.

Flight paths between Canada and Europe have been busy lately, and figurative transatlantic distances are closing fast. As Canada’s relations with the noisiest neighbour to the south stretch and fray, Canadian prime minister Mark Carney is forging alliances with the EU so close that the bloc is apparently inventing new membership categories.

As an American residing in Europe who is also a Canadian leader with robust approval ratings, Marsch is watching. To him, it feels right.

“I’ve always thought Canada was a little bit more European than the US anyway. Right?” Marsch tells the Guardian. “But certainly now there’s enough happening politically and economically that you would say, we’re looking much more like that. There’s talk of [Canada becoming an associate EU member] even actually happening . I like that aspect.

“There’s a uniqueness to Canada in terms of how truly multiethnic this country has become. You can see that Canada is not just a North American country any more, you know? That bodes well for our sport and for the makeup of our team, the makeup of our fans.”

Having led Canada’s men to historic highs at this summer’s World Cup, Marsch is feeling his way into his second act in the job. Some of his sideline displays – we’ll get to that meme – may have irked outsiders, especially in his homeland, during the tournament. Yet, having extended for four more years, Marsch is someone an overwhelming majority of Canadians are happy to have at the helm. There are more than a few cross-points between Marsch and Carney.

“My impression is that first of all, he is a really smart guy, but a really normal guy,” Marsch says of Carney, who attended a number of Canada’s World Cup matches. “Sometimes you meet a US president, and you’re overwhelmed, maybe by their presence, the position itself. I’ve met Clinton, George Bush Sr, Obama, Trump, Biden. Oh, and Carter. Six in person. Carney, compared to all of them, the closest would be Obama. A real air of intelligence, but a real air of being a regular guy. I think that that’s perfect for this country and this moment.

“He has shown great support for us. I made a joke with him that ‘I heard you’re an Everton fan?’ and he goes, ‘Yeah’. And I go, ‘I’m sorry about that’. He replies: ‘Why does everybody say that? Everybody has to pick their team and stick by them.’ I said, ‘I appreciate that you don’t switch from Everton to Arsenal or Liverpool, like everybody else’. There’s something so genuine [about] that. Could a president of the US ever be an Everton fan? No chance.”

Circumstances, as well as natural impulses, have led Marsch to play statesman during this prolonged cooling of relations between Canada and his home country. He’s been defiant – lashing out at Donald Trump’s “51st state” barbs – then more deft. Sometimes, especially when it comes to the US Soccer Federation he said led him on with a job offer only to renege, he finds it hard to hide his disdain.

This window is the start of turning the page to the next phase of his Canada project. He admits, with a chuckle, that the four years stretching ahead feel long but there are imminent goals – a first trophy in 25 years, cracking and consolidating inside the world’s top 24.

A win over Chile in Toronto and 2-0 win over Peru here on Saturday afternoon in games billed as The Homecoming made for a solid start. New caps have been handed out. Key players arrived thriving in new surroundings, none more than Jonathan David at Atlético Madrid. Extended injury absences and the awkward non-attendance of captain Alphonso Davies (skipping the window to honeymoon) have been overcome.

But Tuesday’s clash with the US in Saint Paul means more American questions are coming. Looking back, the Folarin Balogun affair feels absolutely tailor-made for a Marschian verdict. He, of course, has thoughts.

“Well, this is a deep conversation,” he leans back. “We, as Americans, have been inundated with propaganda since we were young. We’re the No 1 country in the world, we deserve everything, we dominate everything, No 1 in every aspect of life. This is what we’ve been told. So, when things happen and we don’t feel like we’re in control of it … we feel like we deserve to be treated differently because we’re Americans. That is one of the things that infuriates the rest of the world about Americans. And Americans don’t know that if they don’t ever leave the country.

“So what I feel when the Balogun ruling happens is that would never happen in any other country in the world, and this is why everyone around the world hates America. That was proven to be so. The US had had a good World Cup, was doing well. All that switched in one moment. But do I think that that’s about corruption and unfairness? The problem is, football is inundated with this kind of stuff.”

The meme is another World Cup leftover. “I’ve had all kinds of people ask me what it was, was it a meat slicer?” he says of his sideline gyrations during their match against Qatar. The incident spawned a gif which has been used plenty in the Marsch family WhatsApp since. “I don’t know what I’m doing sometimes. As soon as I’ve done it, I’m like: ‘Why did I do that? I’m such an idiot’.”

He doesn’t feel fooled, however, by the sport’s latest, arguably greatest, modern corruption crisis. Defeats to Manchester City in 2022-23 didn’t help the Leeds United side Marsch had managed when they missed safety by five points. That campaign is not one of the “sham” seasons which were part of the damning verdict against City last week. But he’s adamant the unfairness extended to his time in England.

“I think Man City should be punished severely. I think they should have to go down, and by the way, everyone knew about it. Everyone knew,” says Marsch, who also pointed to Everton and Nottingham Forest later being deducted points for issues in the same season when Leeds were relegated below both.

“That summer [2022], us and Man City were the only teams that said we made money. For us, we did make money, because we sold Raphinha, we sold Kalvin Phillips [to City]. We had a lot left over from what we bought. At the time, we weren’t in a position financially to not save. Our ownership didn’t have deep pockets. Whereas when Man City says this, I was literally like, ‘Are you kidding me? Is this some kind of joke?’

“When they said they got Erling Haaland for £52m, it’s like: ‘Yeah, OK, sure!’ So, I knew there were inconsistencies in it, but what can you do? You just put your arms in the air and go, ‘This is football’.”

The US had had a good World Cup, was doing well. All that switched in one moment. But do I think that that’s about corruption and unfairness? The problem is, football is inundated with this kind of stuff.”

The meme is another World Cup leftover. “I’ve had all kinds of people ask me what it was, was it a meat slicer?” he says of his sideline gyrations during their match against Qatar. The incident spawned a gif which has been used plenty in the Marsch family WhatsApp since. “I don’t know what I’m doing sometimes. As soon as I’ve done it, I’m like: ‘Why did I do that? I’m such an idiot’.”

He doesn’t feel fooled, however, by the sport’s latest, arguably greatest, modern corruption crisis. Defeats to Manchester City in 2022-23 didn’t help the Leeds United side Marsch had managed when they missed safety by five points. That campaign is not one of the “sham” seasons which were part of the damning verdict against City last week. But he’s adamant the unfairness extended to his time in England.

“I think Man City should be punished severely. I think they should have to go down, and by the way, everyone knew about it. Everyone knew,” says Marsch, who also pointed to Everton and Nottingham Forest later being deducted points for issues in the same season when Leeds were relegated below both.

“That summer [2022], us and Man City were the only teams that said we made money. For us, we did make money, because we sold Raphinha, we sold Kalvin Phillips [to City]. We had a lot left over from what we bought. At the time, we weren’t in a position financially to not save. Our ownership didn’t have deep pockets. Whereas when Man City says this, I was literally like, ‘Are you kidding me? Is this some kind of joke?’

“When they said they got Erling Haaland for £52m, it’s like: ‘Yeah, OK, sure!’ So, I knew there were inconsistencies in it, but what can you do? You just put your arms in the air and go, ‘This is football’.”

articles.title: NRL grand final 2026: Sydney Roosters 19-18 Newcastle Knights – as it happened
articles.summary: Roosters hold off brave Knights in classic grand final in Sydney James Tedesco wins Clive Churchill medal as Roosters win 16th title NRLW: Roosters blow away Broncos to claim third premiership The first wave of Knights successes came against a backdrop of uncertainty about what a post-industrial future might mean for the steel city. Two decades on, for better or worse, working-class Newcastle is now safer, more confident and outward-looking; also more expensive and exclusive. DCE has spoken to Channel 9 about the enormity of the occasion. To be honest, just because of the occasion of the grand final, it’s been really easy to put it to the side. I feel like the moment I’ve made it all about myself at any time of my career, it’s never really worked out too well. So real team focus today. Yeah, really good. The longer turnaround I feel really helped us. We were able to get extra recovery in and then build our week really nicely. So I feel like it was a great week of preparation. And now it’s just trusting that to go out and play… it’s not about any storyline for us tonight. It’s just about getting the job done. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Thank you for joining me tonight. And be sure to stay tuned to these pages in the coming weeks for live coverage of the Rugby League World Cup, which kicks off in just 11 days with Australia v New Zealand at Allianz Stadium, Sydney.

For now I’ll leave you with the words of Angus Fontaine, who was front and centre at Accor Stadium on another golden night for the Sydney Roosters .

James Tedesco offers a few quick words of thanks then makes his way over to his teammates and hoists the Provan-Summons Trophy to the sky. Confetti rains down on the victorious Roosters. Simply The Best gets a second airing of the night. Another remarkable NRL campaign draws to a close.

The Roosters players stride onto the dais in order, some with infants under their arms, to accept the acclaim of the crowd and receive their premiership rings.

Firstly, I’d just like to thank the NRL and all the sponsors for making this year even bigger and better than before. I congratulate the Roosters. I’ll just say thank you to our boys, to our club, to our fans. What a ride. Obviously so proud to be here, proud to represent you people. We’re still chasing that premiership. To the Roosters, congratulations, class outfit deserving of tonight. Enjoy it boys.

Adam Gee and the rest of the match officials accept their medallions. They were fortunate to have little to do tonight but they kept the game under control at all times. Well done those men.

Nearly 400m with ball in hand, 14 tackle breaks, an offload, and two kicks that led to drop-outs, the Sydney skipper is a very well deserved player of the match.

The flipside of DCE’s delight is Kalyn Ponga’s despair. “It hurts,” he tells Johnathan Thurston, “it hurts so much. I know we did them proud, but the ultimate goal is to win a comp. Can’t thank them enough for their support. We’ll be back.”

Cherry-Evans salutes the crowd as a microphone is offered in his direction. “I didn’t do anything,” he demurs, “we did it! Thank you so much, everyone here tonight. I’m so grateful. Thank you so much for the support. It’s been an amazing journey. I’m so lucky.

I had so much belief in this club, the players, the coach. This is what it’s all about. And we did it. And I’m so, so proud to be here, and I just can’t wait to go see my family.”

In truth, Sydney could – should – have won by a cricket score. That they didn’t is credit to Newcastle’s resilience. From about 20 minutes into the contest they had their backs to the wall, hardly able to exit their own half, accepting punishment after punishment yet standing straight back up and asking for more.

Fittingly, the 2026 grand final ends with the ball in the hands of Daly Cherry-Evans. 15 years after his first premiership ring he bows out of the NRL with a second, this time as the oldest player in grand final history.

79 mins: DCE grubbers through to Ponga. Newcastle have 85m to travel to find a point or more.

78 mins: With the restart set Newcastle go from right to left and left to right through hands, looking for Ponga throughout. Sydney scramble, the bomb goes up on the last, and Tedesco takes an absolutely wonderful catch on his knees. Blimey, what a competition. It never fails.

Ponga wins a penalty for being tackled in the air as he marks the latest DCE bomb. Surely this is Newcastle’s last opportunity. There’s desperation with ball in hand, offloads, runners looking for gaps, Gagai is busy, Manuleleua is urgent, but it’s all about Ponga. He runs on the last, there are bodies outside him on the left, it comes to Marzhew with two to beat in the corner – he steps inside, rolls, breaks through the tackles – and he’s over! No way! No effing way!

76 mins: Coming out of defence, the Knights cannot land a glove on the Roosters. There is no way on earth they can bridge this gap with just four minutes remaining.

74 mins: Newcastle’s defence has been heroic! They have repelled runner after runner and survived all manner of aerial sorties into the corners. Sydney look odds on to score on multiple occasions but the white wall holds firm and by the last Nawaqanitawase is squeezed of space with Tedesco assisting for the umpteenth time.

72 mins: Sydney belt the penalty from halfway to the 30m line. Then on tackle three Collins thinks he’s crossed one-out, with white jerseys hanging off him. The decision onfield is no try, confirmed by the TMO. The Roosters come again and on the last Tedesco chips to the right corner. Nawaqanitawase marks it, the ball spills loose and Toia crosses! But again the decision is no try, and again it’s upheld by the TMO, but play will restart with Sydney ball after the rugby-bound winger was tackled mid-air.

71 mins: Newcastle fail to kick the restart the required 10m and the Roosters load a few more cartridges into their shotgun.

Sydney pound downfield and with just ten minutes left on the clock DCE, the oldest grand finalist in history, uses all his experience to dab over a simple field goal from 20m to extend his side’s lead beyond a converted try.

69 mins: The Knights are so exhausted their brains are scrambled. Another sortie down the right ends with a recovered kick that is hacked for a second time by Gagai that floats harmlessly to Nawaqanitawase in-goal.

68 mins: Sydney reload but Toia fumbles now! Is the ball getting slippery as dew sets in? Is the pitch cutting up? Newcastle are still breathing… just.

66 mins: To rub salt in the wound Foketi, and the soon-to-be Clive Churchill Medalist James Tedesco, make yards at will. Another bomb goes towards the right corner, Newcastle don’t deal with it, but Sydney are unable to hoover up the crumbs on the deck and the Knights survive, for now.

65 mins: For the first time in an age Newcastle are in A1 attacking position – and Sharpe grasses a dolly at first receiver. You could hear the groans from the Hunter in every state in Australia.

64 mins: A glimmer of hope for the Knights? For four tackles they labour out of defence but then they revert to type, chancing their arm, jinking, offloading, Manuleleua is important, as is Graham, and they get a repeat set when Smith knocks on trying to tackle Ponga.

62 mins: Something has got to change, and fast, if the Knights are going to get back into this. Right now they are drowning, not waving.

The Roosters are coming alright. This is irresistible. Time and again tonight they have wasted red zone possession and this time they get the rub of the green. DCE grubbers through the line, it ricochets off the upright to Tedesco, he sees a glimmer of space on the right, and that’s all Mark Nawaqanitawase needs to dash around the outside of Marzhew and dive over in the right corner.

58 mins: Whyte stomps through the middle of Accor Stadium like Godzilla trampling a small central business district. The send ends with a forced dropout, which of course is followed by Daniel Tupou taking a speccy on the left wing. The Roosters are coming.

56 mins: If Newcastle thought their task couldn’t get any harder, on comes Whyte for his second stint to hammer the defensive line from the restart. The Knights hold out but how do they turn the tide their way? With ball in hand they are so slow to get back onside it’s almost impossible to offer anything creative. If the Roosters avoid errors it’s hard to see this lead doing anything but growing.

The retreating Knights defence infringes off the ball and Walker is invited to kick his side in front for the first time this grand final. 30m out, just to the left of the uprights, and he makes no mistake.

Finally Sydney have control of the scoreboard to reflect their dominance of the football.

54 mins: At half-time Sydney were clearly instructed to run and offload more, and it is paying dividends. Walker in particular has impacted the game more, Tedesco and Nawaqanitawase are running the Knights ragged, and it only seems like a matter of time before Newcastle are unable to keep their guard up.

articles.title: Purchase of field aims to expand 'green lung'
articles.summary: It is hoped the prospective sale provides a haven for wildlife in an urban area.
articles.content:
The purchase of fields in St Clements aims to provide space for wildlife in the urban environment

Conservationists have said they are planning to buy a field to extend a "green lung" in one of Jersey's most built-up parishes.

The National Trust for Jersey said it had secured the rights to acquire the land near Maupertuis Farm in St Clement and hoped to complete the purchase shortly.

A green lung is an area of fields, parkland or vegetation within an otherwise urban area, providing space for wildlife and helping to reduce pollution.

The trust previously raised £50,000 in 37 days to buy a nearby field on Samares Lane in 2021.

The trust said the latest acquisition would help preserve the agricultural heritage of Maupertuis Farm and the surrounding area.

Chief executive Alan Le Maistre said green spaces were becoming "ever more precious" and protecting them was particularly important in densely developed parts of the island.

"It is a privilege to have the opportunity to extend this green lung for both the wildlife and people of the area," he said.

The National Trust for Jersey, which celebrated its 90th anniversary in August , manages about 1,800 vergées of land across the island.

It invited people who want to support the latest acquisition to contact the charity directly.

articles.title: Max Verstappen wins his first race of season at Bahrain GP after rain delay causes chaos – as it happened
articles.summary: Max Verstappen broke his 2026 duck as wet weather caused chaos in Malaysia and George Russell saw his title hopes go up in smoke Tyres: Tyre degradation has been one of the big talking points throughout the weekend, and with the rain threatening to shake things up, it is worth taking another look at what could prove crucial if the track starts to dry. The circuit’s naturally abrasive surface is already putting plenty of stress through the tyres, while the extreme track temperatures had been adding to the problem too. With the conditions cooling, that is less of a concern for now. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Big congratulations to Max, what a tough race that was. Obviously, we had the wrong call at the beginning which was so difficult.

I could see everyone pulling away and I could see on the screen that I was a minute down, and I thought that was kind of race over for us.

But I just kept my head down. The guys did a great job with the pit stops. Obviously, lots of tyre changes, lots of chasing.

And honestly, of all the years I’ve been here, this is the best race we’ve had here, but particularly because of this crowd. So, a big thank you to everyone.

I think today was the maximum we could have done, massive congrats to Max and Red Bull for their incredible weekend.

On our side, work to do but happy to come away with P2. Hopefully we will come back in the future to Malaysia.

It’s a really nice one [win] after the year we’ve had and the progression we have made. I’m incredibly proud of everyone. Just super nice to win here.

It was very hectic with a lot of different things at the start – no power [on the first formation lap in the rain] because you have to wait for the power to kick in.

We made the right call with the intermediates. After that, step by step we moved out way forward.

From there, once we could do our own race then we had the Safety Car but we kept it all under control.

Verstappen finally has his first win of the season, while Antonelli leaves with an even bigger championship lead after a race that threatened to change everything. For Russell, though, it was absolute heartbreak, with his late retirement dealing a huge blow to his title hopes.

Hamilton and Ferrari may have got their tyre calls badly wrong, but somehow they still walk away with a double result in third and fourth – a remarkable recovery given how the strategy unfolded.

And there is still some business to settle after the chequered flag. Albon and Norris are both facing post-race investigations for allegedly driving erratically, so the final classification could yet change.

Max Verstappen has done it again. The last time F1 raced in Malaysia, back in 2017, it was Verstappen who stood on the top step – and nine years later, he has repeated the feat.

Verstappen holds off championship leader Kimi Antonelli to take victory after a race that had absolutely everything: rain, Safety Cars, strategic gambles, late drama and a frantic final few laps. It is also Red Bull’s first Grand Prix victory of the season.

Kimi Antonelli comes in second and Lewis Hamilton – what a day he has had – rounds out the podium.

Lap 54/55: Antonelli is now more than a second behind Verstappen, but cannot afford to ease off too much – Hamilton is lurking behind and would love the chance to put the championship leader under pressure.

Further back, Leclerc is all over Hadjar in the fight for fourth. And there it is! Leclerc makes the move into Turn 1 and gets past Hadjar.

Lap 53/55: Russell’s retirement and Norris’ earlier off have shuffled the order once again, with Alonso now up to eighth. Norris has already recovered one position, getting past Lindblad to move back into the points.

Hulkenberg is up to ninth but is under serious pressure as the laps tick away. He will have to defend for his life if he is to hold on to that position.

Up front, Verstappen remains comfortably in the lead, but there is a change behind him. Hamilton makes his move on Hadjar down the main straight and takes P3.

Lap 52/55: Verstappen times the restart perfectly, launching away from the Safety Car and immediately opening a gap to Antonelli. It was a smart move from the Dutchman, while Antonelli understandably takes a more cautious approach after seeing Russell retire.

There is plenty going on behind, too. Lawson and Piastri are battling it out, with the McLaren struggling for grip on the hard tyres.

Lap 50/55: Norris is not allowed to regain those positions under the Safety Car, so he drops back to P11. He can count himself fortunate, too, with Stroll showing plenty of sportsmanship by allowing him back on to the track after the off. Norris was caught out as the frontrunners backed up behind the stricken Russell, leaving him with nowhere to go and sending him on to the gravel.

Speaking of Russell, the marshals are now pushing his Mercedes away from the track.

Lap 50/55: With the field still behind the Safety Car, Russell suddenly pulls over on the main straight. At almost the same moment, Norris slides off into the gravel.

Russell immediately puts his hands on his helmet. If this is a retirement, it could be devastating for his championship hopes. And now Russell is climbing out of the car. His race is over, and with the Mercedes stopped on track, the race cannot restart just yet. Mercedes are reporting a power-unit issue, and this could prove hugely costly in the championship fight.

Lap 49/55: Perez has now caught up with the pack and successfully unlapped himself.

Hopefully, we won’t have to wait much longer before the Safety Car comes in and we can finally get this race back underway.

Lap 48/55: The lapped cars are finally being released, with Sainz the first to get the call to unlap himself.

Sainz was caught in the middle of the lead pack, so it appears Race Control is not waiting for the entire field to bunch up before clearing the lapped traffic. Perez and Bortoleto have also been given permission to unlap themselves, although neither has reached the main pack just yet.

Lap 47/55: The Safety Car remains on track as marshals continue working to clear Albon’s stranded Williams.

Once the car is safely removed, attention will turn to the lapped drivers. They have not yet been released, with the field still needing to bunch up before Race Control can allow them to unlap themselves.

articles.title: Dining across the divide: ‘Without being patronising, I think as he grows older he’ll tune in to the damage “free speech” can do’
articles.summary: Did a Tory voter who opposes all censorship offend a leftwinger concerned about how people treat one another? • Want to meet someone from across the divide? Click here to find out how Ted, 24 , London Occupation Works for a thinktank Continue reading...
articles.content:
Did a Tory voter who opposes all censorship offend a leftwinger concerned about how people treat one another?

Want to meet someone from across the divide? Click here to find out how

Amuse bouche Ted does am dram with Loughborough’s Festival Players – probably his biggest part was in The Railway Children in 2019

Voting record Mostly Labour; will vote tactically for Lib Dem, but after Nick Clegg really has to think about it

Amuse bouche Nicky’s mum and dad met at a Louis Armstrong concert in Malawi. He was helping with independence and her grandparents ran a hostel on the top of Zomba mountain

Nicky He was a really lovely, warm, enthusiastic human being. Obviously considerably younger than me.

Ted She was basically what I expected. It was a very pleasant evening.

Ted I am a free speech absolutist – I don’t believe in any restrictions whatsoever. Things such as the Communications Act 2003 and the Online Safety Act 2023 are resulting in huge numbers of arrests for speech offences. You start by criminalising things most of us would agree were abhorrent, but it’s the thin end of the wedge. You end up seeing people arrested for perfectly valid points of view, things that are relatively tame.

Nicky I challenged him on a lot of things, and he did have caveats. For instance, he had quite strong views on abortion, but he didn’t necessarily believe people making that difficult decision should be hounded. When you pushed him on detail, on the moral implications, on the silent mental damage of unchecked free speech, he did say there’s a time and a place for saying what you think. Without sounding patronising, I think as he grows older he will tune into the damage you can do.

Ted She raised the point of people in her family who would be caused serious mental harm if others were allowed to express their opinions freely to them. I think being able to take offence is not a right, or certainly more important is the right to say what you want. I want to know who holds abhorrent views, rather than it be pushed underground. I want to look my enemy in the face.

Nicky If you stand in front of somebody and diminish them, and do that enough, the toll that takes means there will be suicides and anguish that you will never see the numbers on. Do I believe the government should tell us everything we need to do and say? No. We are in a democracy. But we should also treat others as we’d wish to be treated ourselves.

Nicky On healthcare, he was spouting the example of Norwegian and other countries’ semi-insurance policies, and I said: “This just drives us to the US position.” I’m a base-level healthcare believer: there’s a duty of care and any emergency should be dealt with. And he agreed with that.

Ted I expressed my desire to abolish the NHS and replace it with a social insurance model. This would still have provision for free treatment at the point of need, but people would pay through insurance systems, and they would choose the level of cover they’ve got. Those models deliver far better outcomes for patients.

Nicky He loves the monarchy. Look, given the chance, I’d probably vote “no” to keeping them. But I do respect the fact they bring in huge amounts of tourism and I don’t really resent state payments, so long as it’s for work. I haven’t got an issue with the security cost, either. But do I think people should be born into privilege and power? No. He did say, at one point, “When is enough? For these ultra-rich people, what will be enough?” That showed a sensitive side, and I really warmed to him.

Ted It’s not the people, it’s the institution that I love. I think it’s fundamental to the system of governance of this country, which led to us being so strong. Not just the monarchy, but the constitution as a whole and a parliament that is sovereign. It’s worked for 1,000 years.

Ted We both said it had been a really interesting and fun evening and we were glad we’d done it.

Nicky He was a lovely human being. I think he’ll evolve – he’s one to watch!

articles.title: Max Verstappen wins chaotic F1 Bahrain GP in Malaysia after rain causes farcical scenes
articles.summary: First win of season for Dutchman after long rain delay Heartbreak for Russell as power units struggle in weather Max Verstappen won a chaotic Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia with a dominant drive for Red Bull, his team’s first win of the season, beating the Mercedes of Kimi Antonelli into second. The Italian’s teammate and title rival George Russell was forced to retire with five laps to go leaving the British driver’s title hopes shattered and Antonelli within touching distance of the championship. Lewis Hamilton was third for Ferrari, making a remarkable comeback after a torrid afternoon, starting on the slick rubber tyres in the wet which dropped him as far back as 17th before reviving with a superb drive, including a late pass on Isack Hadjar who finished fifth. Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc was fourth after a race marked by farcical scenes before it was even underway. This season’s engine formula was found sorely wanting the first time it was tested in wet conditions. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Max Verstappen won a chaotic Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia with a dominant drive for Red Bull, his team’s first win of the season, beating the Mercedes of Kimi Antonelli into second. The Italian’s teammate and title rival George Russell was forced to retire with five laps to go leaving the British driver’s title hopes shattered and Antonelli within touching distance of the championship.

Lewis Hamilton was third for Ferrari, making a remarkable comeback after a torrid afternoon, starting on the slick rubber tyres in the wet which dropped him as far back as 17th before reviving with a superb drive, including a late pass on Isack Hadjar who finished fifth. Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc was fourth after a race marked by farcical scenes before it was even underway. This season’s engine formula was found sorely wanting the first time it was tested in wet conditions.

For Antonelli, while Mercedes were no match for Verstappen and Red Bull , he did the required in leading his teammate for most of the race until Russell, who was in third place behind the Italian, had a power unit problem and had to pull off track. Heartbreak for Russell, who suffered an engine problem at the same track where Hamilton endured the similar failure in 2016 which all but cost him the title. Russell’s chances are surely now all but gone. Antonelli has an 84-point lead with seven meetings remaining.

The victory for Verstappen was as dominant as some of his best drives. Having passed Antonelli for the lead in the early stages he was untouchable out front to take the flag nine years after he won in Malaysia in 2017, the last time the circuit held a meeting, for his first win since the Abu Dhabi GP last year.

Before what was a fairly straightforward victory for Verstappen, the new formula was reduced to embarrassing scenes. For the first time these cars had run in the wet a deluge of rain swamped the circuit before the start. The engines, with an almost 50-50 split between electrical and combustion power and already facing fierce criticism all season, proved to have problems that had not been anticipated.

The start had already been delayed by 45 minutes and as the rain eased the cars took to the track for two formation laps. Hamilton, who had a software problem, slowed and then came to a halt on track.

He did restart but was not alone and there were similar issues Affecting other competitors, including Verstappen announcing he could not accelerate and the Ferrari-engined Haas and Cadillac of Esteban Ocon and Valtteri Bottas also stopping. It left the field out of order and in some cases not on the same lap . The start was suspended, with the cars returning to the pit lane.

A further delay of 53 minutes ensued as the cars were re-sorted into grid order and the FIA uploaded new software parameters to the cars. The issue was caused, it appears, by the cars being off throttle too long in the wet, the turbo spooling down. Subsequently all the electrical power was being used. The engine was then unable to produce enough power to be within the FIA regulation, preventing it from re-accelerating. A trap that had not apparently been foreseen.

None of which takes the sheen off Verstappen’s victory, representing an extraordinary turnaround delivered with no little fortitude. For the opening half of the season the car had been an absolute handful to drive and even Verstappen, for all his skill, struggled to master it. Since then Red Bull have delivered upgrades perhaps beyond expectations. After being almost a bit-part player for much of the season, a win in Malaysia was a mighty achievement.

When racing was finally under way, Verstappen had a terrible start and was passed by Antonelli, while Russell made a brilliant getaway from seventh to claim second into the first corner.

Struggling for grip on slick rubber, Hamilton fell backwards, while Verstappen recovered to stay with the two Mercedes. Verstappen caught Russell, who was struggling for grip on the fourth lap. Showing great pace the Dutch driver claimed second and set off after Antonelli. Verstappen was right behind Antonelli at a safety-car restart and the pair went wheel to wheel through the first three corners before the Dutchman edged ahead. Russell took advantage too, cutting past his teammate to claim second.

From which point Verstappen held the race in his hands, while Antonelli proved once more to have more pace than Russell and swept past his teammate on lap 21.

Hamilton, showing huge determination, moved through the field and was up to fifth by lap 29 and made a late pass on Hadjar to claim a podium place. While Verstappen held complete control to the flag the race still held late drama when a despondent Russell was forced to retire. The victory belonged to Verstappen but, in championship terms, Antonelli emerged from Sepang very much on top.

articles.title: Sydney Roosters hold off brave Newcastle Knights to win thrilling NRL grand final
articles.summary: Roosters claim 16th title with 19-18 win in Sydney Mark Nawaqanitawase scores twice after Newcastle held 12-0 lead After a Cinderella season that took them from wooden spooners to a grand final, Newcastle went within a whisker of one of the greatest upsets in rugby league history, falling 19-18 to a dominant Sydney Roosters in the NRL decider in Sydney. Outclassed all day but never outgunned, the Knights scored with minutes to play to set up a thrilling finish, only for the men from Bondi to deny them at the death. Led by their inspirational captain, James Tedesco – a worthy Clive Churchill winner – the Roosters squeezed the life out of Newcastle’s rags to riches story, farewelling their rugby union-bound stars Angus Crichton and Mark Nawaqanitawase in style, the dynamic winger crossing for two spectacular tries as the Roosters’ kicking game nailed the Newcastle underdogs in their own half and didn’t let them out. articles.content:
After a Cinderella season that took them from wooden spooners to a grand final, Newcastle went within a whisker of one of the greatest upsets in rugby league history, falling 19-18 to a dominant Sydney Roosters in the NRL decider in Sydney. Outclassed all day but never outgunned, the Knights scored with minutes to play to set up a thrilling finish, only for the men from Bondi to deny them at the death.

Led by their inspirational captain, James Tedesco – a worthy Clive Churchill winner – the Roosters squeezed the life out of Newcastle’s rags to riches story, farewelling their rugby union-bound stars Angus Crichton and Mark Nawaqanitawase in style, the dynamic winger crossing for two spectacular tries as the Roosters’ kicking game nailed the Newcastle underdogs in their own half and didn’t let them out.

The sonic booms of 80,814 fans fuelled a frantic start, as players fought the urge to shake nerves with early statements. Roosters giant Naufahu Whyte then went head-hunting, rattling the teeth of Dom Young and Kalyn Ponga with heavy shots. But the Knights stayed composed, kicking long and chasing hard. The Roosters soon started to roll though, Sam Walker and Daly Cherry-Evans raining bombs on Ponga.

After going set-for-set for 15 minutes, Whyte looked to have forced the game’s first error, jarring the ball from Tyson Frizell’s grasp. Instead referee Adam Gee blew the game’s first penalty for a high shot. Newcastle charged downfield to 30-metres out and Ponga waved his arms for a set play on the right. But it was a ruse. Like a shark, Francis Manuleleua angled in from the left at warp speed to cross untouched.

The Roosters’ aerial assault had failed, despite Ponga struggling for a clean grab. But after 30 minutes, they finally hit their target as Nawaqanitawase soared, swivelled and touched down. Unfortunately, replays showed a finger-width of displacement. It became a 12-point try when, minutes later, Nawaqanitawase tapped back and Ponga, ghosting behind the lines, scooped it up and raced 95m to score.

At 12-0 up with 48 minutes to play, Newcastle fans were daring to dream. But the Roosters found a riposte with three minutes left in the half, Cherry-Evans dinking a kick for Robert Toia’s sticky fingers. His tap-back found the turf but Nawaqanitawase showed yet more of the invention that has made him a dual-code superstar, smartly dabbing the ball forward off his instep and pouncing to score as it crossed the paint.

As the half-time siren sang, the scoreline defied the statistics. The Roosters had dominated possession 57-43%, charged 286m further and made 30 tackle busts to the Knights’ 11. Both teams had been led from the back, Ponga running for 166m and Tedesco for 178. Despite missing 30 tackles and not one attacking kick, the underdogs were six-points clear. Maybe Lady Luck was a coal miner’s daughter.

The Roosters came out roaring in the second half, hammering at the Knights line. Desperate defence kept them at bay as Salesi Foketi was denied by centimetres and for a while but when hitman Spencer Leniu jolted Young, the Sydney side smelt blood. Leniu re-started the siege, Walker sent it short to Foketi who stood tall and offloaded to Billy Smith and the centre smashed through the tackle to dot down.

All square with 30 minutes to go, Newcastle had tackled themselves to a standstill. Their halves had entered the Roosters’ red zone once, yet been breached 38 times. Having been pounded in the tackle zone all game, they were now being mauled in every collision. The errors started to mount. When their knackered defence infringed, Walker kicked Sydney ahead by 14-12 and coach Trent Robinson went for the jugular.

Again, it was the irrepressible Nawaqanitawase who proved the difference. When a Cherry-Evans grubber hit the goalposts and found the arms of Tedesco, the fullback floated a ball to his winger to spear into the corner for a seventh finals try and an 18-12 lead.

Sensing their final fizzing out, the Knights went into Globetrotters mode, staggering downfield in spurts and sideways moves, only for Fletcher Sharpe to knock on cold.

That got the Roosters fans clucking and when 37-year-old Cherry-Evans, the oldest grand finalist in history, calmly slotted a field goal a few minutes later, the crowd of 80,814 suddenly swarmed with red, white and blue, crowing at a sniff of a 16th title. Even then the Knights wouldn’t lie down. They punched upfield, surging on fumes, and somehow found an overlap for Greg Marzhew to shrug off two men and cross.

At 19-18, the NRL had another grandstand finish in their grand final. The Roosters kicked long and the Knights had a set to scramble. But after a season that strained credulity, reality bit. Their magic ran dry and the bag of tricks came up empty. The Roosters, ruthless all season, squeezed hard and the men from Newcastle snapped. Newcastle had given fans a fairytale run but it was the Chooks taking home the title.
