articles.content:
LD is the submissive to Lady Alice’s dominatrix – and it has been a revelation for them both

I have cerebral palsy and live with my parents. Lady Alice is a delicious secret

I met Lady Alice on X. We aren’t lovers or friends. She is my mistress and has complete control over me. I am hers to use however she pleases and she expects nothing less than absolute obedience. I don’t pay Lady Alice a fee, though I might pay for a service she needs such as a pedicure. These payments are “tributes”, tokens of respect and devotion.

I am 43 and use a wheelchair because I have cerebral palsy. I live with my elderly parents; they cut up my food and wash me. Lady Alice is a precious secret.

I never felt in control and hated my body. I had sexual impulses, but because I have ornamental hips that I can’t thrust and erectile dysfunction, I’m not equipped for sex in the conventional sense. I had a “friend with benefits” 20 years ago. We had two – admittedly fun – meetings that unfortunately lacked any real penetration.

In our sessions she makes me feel like there’s nothing wrong with me, as though I was simply born to kneel and be her “stress toy”. I need help cutting up food due to limited control over my fingers, but I am able to crawl and get down on my knees for Lady Alice.

Most of our sessions happen online, but recently, I flew over 400 miles to kneel at Lady Alice’s feet. My father took me on the journey because I can’t travel alone, but he didn’t know who I was meeting. He thought he was dropping me off at a friend’s house.

The setting for my ordeal wasn’t a dark, oppressive dungeon filled with chains, but a light and comfortable living room. Many might wonder why I’d want to be dominated when I must already experience enough pain and humiliation being disabled. But when I’m in a session, I don’t feel disabled. I feel human, happy.

Put it this way: would you rather feel as though your life was ruled by brain damage or a beautiful woman who enjoys playing with your flawed body and appreciates your devotion?

After years of sexual apathy, I became something of a carnally incontinent alley cat

Most of my sessions with LD happen via video call. He kneels for me, wearing his collar, and I tell him erotic stories or make him masturbate. I know the phrases that send him into a blissful state of submissiveness. This is my ultimate goal – in the BDSM community, this is called subspace. For submissive people, this feeling is more sought after than an orgasm.

LD is unbelievably respectful. Many so-called submissive men can’t truly surrender and really only wish to serve themselves. LD puts me first, always.

I discovered that I had an aptitude for consensual humiliation three years ago, rather unexpectedly. I started hormone replacement therapy and the transformation was almost instant: after years of sexual apathy, I became a carnally incontinent alley cat.

I got on the apps, and alongside the conventional profiles were some rather strange ones: requests from men describing themselves as “pay pigs” wishing to be “financially drained”; others wanted me to tell them they were sexually inadequate; and there are an ungodly number of boys begging to be “pegged”. A self-professed “financial domination” addict in Dundee became my unlikely mentor. I grilled him on specifics: how to present myself online; how to monetise it; what to share; what to withhold?

LD and I have only met once in person, but more important to both of us is our daily relationship. I’ve seen him bloom. Having life restricted due to limited mobility is so frustrating and unpleasant. I want so much more for LD than he currently has. He’s a fiercely intelligent, creative man. Through being “owned” by me, he has another lens to view himself. This inspires him. Before we met, I don’t think LD had much of an outlet for his sexuality. I know how energising discovering this side of yourself can be.

LD and I have only met once in person, but more important to both of us is our daily relationship. I’ve seen him bloom. Having life restricted due to limited mobility is so frustrating and unpleasant. I want so much more for LD than he currently has. He’s a fiercely intelligent, creative man. Through being “owned” by me, he has another lens to view himself. This inspires him. Before we met, I don’t think LD had much of an outlet for his sexuality. I know how energising discovering this side of yourself can be.

articles.title: Sydney Roosters blow away Brisbane Broncos to claim third NRLW premiership
articles.summary: Dominant Roosters run in seven tries in 30-6 romp at Accor Stadium Tarryn Aiken wins Karyn Murphy medal as player of match The Sydney Roosters ruined the farewell of NRLW great Ali Brigginshaw by blitzing the Brisbane Broncos in the grand final as the Tricolours completed their perfect season with a 30-6 victory clinched by a six-tries-to-none first half. The Roosters’ third premiership closes the gap on the four won by the Broncos, with the two most successful clubs in the NRLW’s nine-year history now sharing seven titles. But this season was the best the competition has seen, after the Roosters won all 11 regular season matches and their two finals. Continue reading...
articles.content:
The Sydney Roosters ruined the farewell of NRLW great Ali Brigginshaw by blitzing the Brisbane Broncos in the grand final as the Tricolours completed their perfect season with a 30-6 victory clinched by a six-tries-to-none first half.

The Roosters’ third premiership closes the gap on the four won by the Broncos, with the two most successful clubs in the NRLW’s nine-year history now sharing seven titles. But this season was the best the competition has seen, after the Roosters won all 11 regular season matches and their two finals.

Sunday’s win in glorious afternoon sunshine at Accor Stadium corrected the blip of last season’s decider, when the Broncos upset the Roosters . That anomaly is the Tricolours’ only loss since August 2024, underscoring the dominance of John Strange’s team in recent years.

Retiring Roosters forward Millie Elliott said that result pushed them to even greater heights. “Everyone knows what that felt like and we definitely used that as motivation all season, not just in this game, all season,” she said. “And we worked so hard, I take my hat off to Strangey and the coaching staff, they really left no stone unturned this year and we wanted to put in a performance like that.”

Roosters halves Tarryn Aiken – who was awarded the Karyn Murphy medal – and Jocelyn Kelleher outperformed Brigginshaw and the out-of-sorts Jesse Southwell to deliver a statement to Jillaroos selectors preparing to name the squad for the World Cup beginning later this month. But the Roosters’ inspirational captain Isabelle Kelly and their marauding pack were all brilliant as the Tricolours proved far too good.

The opening stages were marred by errors from both sides – including two Roosters mistakes direct from kick-offs – but Kelly’s side quickly rose to an occasion utterly missed by the Broncos. A fourth-minute try was a marvel of keeping the ball alive as winger Jayme Fressard found Kelleher, whose pinpoint cross-field kick looped over opposite winger Kerri Johnson for Brydie Parker to catch and score.

Kelleher might have been the least recognised half on the field, behind her teammate Aiken and the Broncos’ pair of Brigginshaw and Southwell, but she was the game’s most influential player in the early stages. Her soaring bomb embarrassed Brisbane fullback Tamika Upton, who collided with her winger Julia Robinson in her attempt to field the ball.

The Broncos escaped the ensuing set, but found themselves even further behind soon after when Aiken was fortunate in having her grubber rebound off Johnson back into her hands. Minutes later, a Kelleher kick forced another error from the Broncos, and immediately afterwards Aiken put captain Kelly through for the Roosters’ third try. Aiken and Kelly combined again not long after, when the halfback kicked across the field for Kelly, who quickly offloaded to Fressard to score another marvellous four-pointer.

Brigginshaw was lucky to stay on the field when she dived in on Aiken’s standing leg in that play, an obvious sign of frustration in the 36-year-old’s final game. This afternoon should have been a celebration of Brigginshaw’s career, but her Broncos imploded. By the end of the first half they had 25% of possession and completed just three of 10 sets. Run metres were 830 to 259, tackle breaks 17 to six.

There was simply no relief for the Broncos. After another Kelleher bomb, Olivia Kernick and Rima Butler picked up Upton and forced her back into the in-goal.The next set the Roosters were in again, a spread right found Kelly – popping up on the opposite side – who put Parker in for her acrobatic second. Aiken then found Amber Hall with a short ball to make the half-time score 26-0.

A miraculous try-saver from Upton at the start of the second half could not trigger a comeback, and Parker secured her hat-trick with 15 minutes to go. A try from Southwell in the 63rd minute, after Upton finally found some space down the middle, was the only blemish on an otherwise immaculate day for the Roosters.

A late handling error from Brigginshaw, challenged unsuccessfully by the Broncos, was anything but a fairytale finish for the NRLW’s greatest player. She was in tears at the end, embracing her teammates and family.

Instead, it was the Roosters celebrating as the final siren rang out around a stadium by now half-full, the joy of victory bittersweet for Elliott and fullback Corban Baxter, who hang up the boots while still at the top of their game.

articles.title: My friends are spouting conspiracy theories – what should I say? | Ask Annalisa Barbieri
articles.summary: You can be curious about others’ beliefs without compromising your own Recently, I had a conversation with a friend who explained that her ill health was down to reasons I would describe as dubious. Taking certain supplements and changing her diet have significantly improved her health. Good for her. However, she was disappointed and a little annoyed that I didn’t share her outrage and wasn’t going to follow her views. I’ve got another friend who thinks cholesterol is a lie and that we should live largely on meat (and supplements). Another went through a sugar causes cancer phase. And another is s ceptical of vaccines. Each of them may be right. They might not. We are learning more about the human body every day. But I was raised by scientists and I want to see a large-scale trial before I get outraged and change the way I live. articles.content:
You can be curious about others’ beliefs without compromising your own

Recently, I had a conversation with a friend who explained that her ill health was down to reasons I would describe as dubious. Taking certain supplements and changing her diet have significantly improved her health. Good for her. However, she was disappointed and a little annoyed that I didn’t share her outrage and wasn’t going to follow her views.

I’ve got another friend who thinks cholesterol is a lie and that we should live largely on meat (and supplements). Another went through a sugar causes cancer phase. And another is s ceptical of vaccines. Each of them may be right. They might not. We are learning more about the human body every day. But I was raised by scientists and I want to see a large-scale trial before I get outraged and change the way I live. Equally, I’m not convinced that a lightly regulated for-profit industry (supplements) is automatically more trustworthy than a highly regulated for-profit one (pharma).

I want to be respectful of their choices and the research they have done into their specific conditions, but for them to respect my beliefs too. The feeling I get is that they think they have the keys to the real intel and I’m being duped by the medical establishment. Or that I’m not a good friend because I don’t believe them.

I’m not sure how to have a respectful conversation about that. I ’d prefer to avoid it, but it comes up often. I find myself making non-committal comments such as “how interesting”. But I know, and they know, I’m sceptical .

But isn’t it OK for your scepticism to still be there? Isn’t this how so many of us get along, skirting over differing views of politics, religion and science? You’re not going to convince them any more than they’ll persuade you, so you need to find common ground.

I went to psychotherapist Ryan Bennett-Clarke, who said: “Healthy relationships don’t need collusion to survive. In fact, healthy discourse can strengthen and invigorate relationships, so long as people are able to listen to each other and demonstrate a desire to hear what the other person is saying. We can be curious and compassionate without having to commit ourselves to something that doesn’t align with our own beliefs and experiences.”

Of course, there are some beliefs that may be harmful for others to hold, but even then you can’t force someone to listen. What I have found often works best is something gentle such as “That’s really interesting, I used to think that until I read XYZ”, and leave it at that. No one is receptive if they are forced into a defensive position. You could even say “Oh really, tell me more”, without having their beliefs tattooed on to you. But if all you have between you are these differences, then a friendship gets harder to sustain. And yes it is difficult to listen to some theories.

Bennett-Clarke thought it was important to remember that “we can retain our right to have our own minds while thinking about the experiences and beliefs of others. Wanting to be understood and similar to others can help us feel less alone in the world. But we can stay in relational contact with someone, even if we don’t share their experiences or beliefs.”

The truth is that the more you dig in with your beliefs the more likely your friends will be to try to convince you of theirs, so be mindful of this. You might also find useful a podcast I made on conflict with resolution expert Gabrielle Rifkind, How to Agree to Disagree . It’s all about how to turn conflict into connection and looks at why being seen to be right isn’t always necessary – even if we are, indeed, right.

articles.content:
The star was just eight when his friend was stabbed. Decades on, he’s ready to talk about that day – how it shaped him, and how, as he becomes a father himself, it will shape him as a dad

“I feel a bit nervous,” confesses John Boyega, as he sits down in front of the camera. “Speaking about it could possibly help. I haven’t revisited this in a long time. Yeah, my heart is just beating.” The Attack the Block and Star Wars actor is talking in the opening scene of a new BBC Two documentary about the killing of 10-year-old schoolboy Damilola Taylor .

On 27 November 2000, Damilola was stabbed in the leg with a broken bottle and left to die in a concrete stairwell, attacked as he walked home from an after-school club at Peckham library in south London. It took six years and three separate trials at the Old Bailey, costing a total of £16m, to secure a manslaughter conviction. His death shocked the nation not only because he was so young, but because all the suspects were also children. Boyega was one of the last people to see Damilola alive. The pair had enjoyed a close friendship since Damilola’s move to the UK from Nigeria in August of that year.

Watching the film at a Bafta screening a few weeks before its premiere, it’s striking how young and vulnerable the 34-year-old actor looks as he talks about the death of his friend. Boyega is more often seen looking assured and confident, be that his impassioned, impromptu address to thousands of people at a Black Lives Matter protest in Hyde Park, posing for the Pirelli calendar, or portraying an African king in a Hollywood movie. Usually he stands tall, with broad shoulders supported by a proud stance. But in revisiting the memories of that day, it feels as if he has almost reverted to the eight-year-old child he was nearly 26 years ago when he found out his friend had died.

A couple of hours later I reconvene with him at BBC New Broadcasting House to discuss the show. In person, Boyega is unassuming, with a calm demeanour and a welcoming smile. He has just returned from a trip to New York fashion week and looks surprisingly fresh-faced for somebody who has not long stepped off a transatlantic flight.

Boyega is sitting comfortably with his father Samson, his mother Abigail and an older cousin. It’s a lively space – Boyega lives in Los Angeles now and I get the impression that everybody is excited to snatch a bit of time with him while he’s in London. We immediately get into a five-way conversation about the criminal proceedings around Damilola’s death. Everybody is talking at once.

The first trial collapsed after the judge ruled that the prosecution’s key witness was unreliable and there was controversy about items of crucial evidence that were excluded from the proceedings. The family closely followed all three trials – in the second, the jury failed to reach a verdict for two of the three defendants on a charge of murder – and there is a sense of frustration at the opportunities missed when it came to bringing the killers to justice.

“You would have thought the influence of the Stephen Lawrence case would have been way stronger, if they had actually learned something. It didn’t come across like that,” Boyega sighs. The police investigation was heavily criticised after it was found to have made a number of significant mistakes.

The whole Boyega family knew Damilola; but the actor has previously said very little about him in public. Boyega has worked consistently since his 2011 debut in sci-fi cult classic Attack The Block, including a gamechanging role as a lead in Disney’s Star Wars franchise. His most recent projects, The Woman King (2022) and They Cloned Tyrone (2023), were both critically acclaimed. He has said that his professional success is in no small part due to being inspired by the way Damilola lived his short life.

He has been deeply involved in the documentary. “The first time I watched a rough cut I was in my living room and it was bright out. Since then, we’ve been watching daily edits, y’know, on a phone, on a laptop, on a little TV. But viewing it in the cinematic setup hits different – it was an emotional hill to get over, seeing the film like that. I feel really impacted by it.” Throughout the 75-minute screening, crying and sniffling could be heard around the room. “It’s one of those films I wouldn’t watch multiple times because of my personal relationship to it, but it’s definitely a film I will refer to – when my child comes of age I will show him this film. You need to know the realities of your lineage.”

O n Damilola Taylor’s first day at Oliver Goldsmith primary school in Peckham, shortly after his arrival in the UK, a teacher assigned Boyega’s sister Grace to be his chaperone. She says in the documentary: “My teacher was like, ‘Grace, there’s a new guy and he’s from Nigeria and obviously you’re Nigerian so you understand the language – you can show him around.’” They became a trio, because Boyega and his sister were inseparable at the time.

“The only reason I was around him a lot was because I was always with my sister – I inherited Damilola,” Boyega tells me, laughing. “I stayed because I found him hilarious.”

His father chimes in with a poignant memory: “John don’t have many friends – at least not boys. John had girls surrounding him. And I remember asking, ‘John, why are you hanging around girls?’ and he said, ‘Dad, boys are dangerous – they’ll beat me up.’” At lunchtimes, the three of them would run around the playground together.

Boyega describes the day Damilola died as a transformational moment for him. “The psychological impact is something that definitely stayed with me, but now it’s expressed through appreciation. Every time I wake up and I’m here, I appreciate it.” He smiles as he says of talking to his friends: “I’ll tell my boys, ‘Hey, a bullet don’t look at you and be like, “You’ve done movies before,” and swerve you!’” As a child, though, his thoughts were less positive. “When I would hear that anybody had been stabbed or whatever, it just felt like it was getting closer and closer and that awareness became part of day-to-day life. I was very scared of that.”

Boyega was eight when Damilola was killed; he had previously thought that death “only happened to old people”. He was bewildered by it – “like when babies fall and everyone goes, ‘Oh my gosh!’ and then the baby [seeing the response] decides to cry? It was like that.” As the news sank in, he found it difficult to comprehend that bad things could happen to good people. “I was trying to compute what that meant. I thought about the practicality of it. The last breath. Does it hurt? I remember with Grace we would have conversations where I’d be like, ‘Do you think death is sleep?’ or, ‘Maybe they go for 20 years and then, they come back?’ It kept me up at night because I was just with the guy, y’know?”

In the aftermath of Damilola’s death, Boyega spent a lot of time at home in his bedroom. Sometimes friends would knock for him and he would tell his mother to relay the message that he didn’t want to go out. “The hand of death is influencing kids to kill kids. I’m like, ‘Damn, I’m a kid, let me stay where I feel the most safe.’ I had a home that granted extreme safety and my parents didn’t shy away from showing concern.”

This played out in many ways, including their choice for his secondary school. Instead of the options in their home borough, he was sent to Westminster City School – almost an hour away by bus. Was getting out of the area a response to Damilola’s death? Boyega’s father answers: “Before John says anything, I went to his teacher when he was going to secondary school and he said to me, ‘Mr Boyega, why do you have to choose Westminster?’ And I never said to him what I saw: that the environment here will corrupt this guy,” he says, pointing at his son. “I saw what was coming, that in the future this environment is going to be very, very dangerous.” This was in 2003. By the end of the decade, 188 teenagers had been murdered on the streets of London.

I direct the conversation back to Boyega. Did he have therapy back then? He lowers his chin and looks at me with a furrowed brow. What he appears to be conveying is there’s no such thing as therapy in an African household – especially not a 1990s African household. We both laugh. At this point I am conscious that my question could easily be construed as a criticism of his parents, who are sitting on the sofa opposite us in the suddenly quite claustrophobic room. We quickly move on.

Over the years there have been numerous documentaries focusing on various aspects of Damilola’s killing, from a 2002 BBC Panorama special to most recently one fronted by broadcaster Yinka Bokinni to mark the 20th anniversary of Damilola’s death. This latest project focuses much of the narrative on the 24 hours leading up to his killing.

We hear from a number of people who were critical to the investigation in its early stages, including the estate maintenance worker who first found Damilola as he lay bleeding in the stairwell. articles.content:
Learning to be one human among many has always been a little lonely and discombobulating. But young people around the world are lonelier than ever. Why?

In September, a Reddit user identifying themselves as a 25-year-old man turned to the r/ForeverAlone subreddit with a question : How do you deal with touch starvation? “It’s becoming obvious to me that I’ll probably be alone forever,” he wrote. He used to be worried about missing out on sex, but now he just misses hugs. Cuddles.

“I don’t have many friends and none with that kind of physical relationship. I don’t really hug family either anymore. Some days, I feel so desperate for a hug with someone I love.”

On another thread, a user identifying as a 20-year-old woman took to the platform to ask if anyone else had experienced university as one of the loneliest times in their lives. “I eat lunch alone, go to class, drive home, study, and repeat,” the user wrote. “Evenings and weekends are the hardest because I crave social connection, but there’s no one to go out with or even talk to.”

Another user, on another subreddit thread , expressed that they had tried to ease their unwanted solitude, but failed. “The loneliness is unbearable,” they wrote. “Is anyone else experiencing this” No question mark. No full stop.

Around the world, young people, according to the 2025 World Health Organization Social Connection Commission report, “feel the loneliest”. Between 17 and 21% of 13-to-29-year-olds report feeling lonely, a greater proportion than any other age group, the report found. Another study , based on a survey of more than 1 million young people from 38 countries, found that youth loneliness had increased in many regions between 2002 and 2022. From Germany to Australia to the UK , studies are showing an uptick in loneliness and social isolation among teenagers and young adults.

That much of the world has produced a generation in which so many regularly feel unable to meet their needs for social connection is a curiosity which has propelled years of work for Dr Michelle Lim.

The act of learning to be one human among many has always been a lonely, discombobulating exercise in parts, she says. But in her new book, The Lonely Generation, the loneliness researcher and clinical psychologist examines exactly what has happened over this century to make many young people even lonelier.

In short, she writes, “It must be said that the nature of childhood has changed dramatically over the past few decades.”

The list of aggravating factors Lim identifies is long: our hyper-competitive education culture, digital technology, the long tail of Covid (“they’re grieving”), the shift towards smaller families, the decline of third spaces , the high cost of living, hybrid working, hybrid learning, the decline of religion, and the rise of automation which means a trip to the supermarket can be conducted entirely without speaking to another human. Young people, she argues, are being offered fewer and fewer opportunities to form meaningful connections.

“What I fear is social atrophy,” she writes. “People are getting used to being alone.”

Lim is one of the world’s pre-eminent loneliness scholars. Alongside her work as a psychologist and researcher, she leads the University of Sydney’s School of Public Health’s Social Health and Wellbeing Group, is CEO of the Australian Ending Loneliness Together campaign, is on a loneliness advisory panel to the World Health Organization and in 2020 cofounded and led the Global Initiative on Loneliness and Connection, which has since expanded to six continents.

In The Lonely Generation, she seeks to dispel myths around loneliness and expound on its many individual and societal consequences. But it is in diagnosing the cause of the “crisis” levels of youth loneliness that she spends the most time. And the first among the culprits she identifies is education.

“The current education systems are built to prioritise academic excellence from children and adolescents,” she writes. And this focus entails “hidden costs”.

After-school tutoring, high-stakes testing and well-intentioned enrolments in extensive extracurricular activities are the hallmarks of a 21st-century education. Lim says that parents tell her: “If I stop, then [my child] will fall behind and I’m not doing the best job I can.”

However, children need rest, free play and empty time in order to practise organic social interactions, says Lim – interactions which are essential to developing their fledgling social skills and a sense of identity outside their family.

“The more time you spend studying, it will come at the expense of [other] important skills,” she says. “We run the risk of raising them to be academically strong, but not socially well-equipped to manage the challenges of adulthood.”

The idea resonates with Usha Makkena, a 22-year-old student at university in Sydney.

“I think when you’re growing up with school, extracurricular activities and then later study and work, a lot of your time can become very structured and goal-oriented,” she says. “Something I realise as I’ve gotten older is that meaningful connection often develops in quite unstructured and almost unproductive times.

“And for me, being very busy certainly didn’t protect me from loneliness.”

Some, solo, walk or sit with earbuds in and eyes fixed on their phones. Across the flight of stairs in the foyer of the main building are cast the words “MAKE NEW CONNECTIONS”.

And the transition from school to university, vocational training or work has always been an inflection point for loneliness, Lim says. Individual young people leave their highly structured environment of high school, with a set cast of characters with whom they are familiar and enter a new world populated by new – and often a vastly greater mass of – people. It is also a time when, often, the desire for a great deal of social interaction and a volume of connection is at its highest. Add to this their prefrontal cortex is still developing and adolescence has yet more years to run its course, the period can be one of flux, confusion, self-questioning and, of course, loneliness.

But this awkward rite of passage is now charged in a new way, says Lim. “Our young people in this generation are living in a world that is very different.”

“You meet new people every day,” says Pathinayake, an exceedingly bright-eyed 20-year-old student from Sri Lanka. But she describes a new social script to developing friendships in 21st century adolescence and young adulthood.

Due to the hybrid online-real life attendance structure to many tutorials and lectures which has proliferated since Covid, it can be difficult to be sure that you may run into the same people with the frequency needed to establish organic connection.

“Sometimes following someone or reacting to something that they post can almost be a substitute for reaching out, even though those interactions don’t meet the same need,” says Makkena over a video call in late September. “And then there’s also that element of comparison.

“For me, when I was already feeling lonely, constantly seeing other people’s friendship groups or social lives could sometimes create the impression that everybody else had found their people and I somehow hadn’t.”

She is, however, wary of narratives which pit technology as the silent assassin of social connection. “It also helped me maintain relationships.”

“Social media has not been an entirely negative development”, writes Lim. While the professor is concerned about the dopamine hit from social media blunting the rewards we feel from other interactions and that, for people who are already lonely, it can embed an aversion to real-life connection, her own research has shown it can fortify young people living in communities that don’t accept them, or help others to learn about the world. “Digital use is not the enemy.”

However, she openly imagines (not happily) a future in which her own daughter might tell her that her best friend is an AI avatar. It does not feel like a big leap from what she already sees in her clinical practice, where she might be helping a young person navigate problems in their romantic relationship only to realise they have never met their boyfriend or girlfriend in real life. “It’s really common,” she says.

These virtual relationships, whether remote between human beings on separate continents or between human and AI avatar, are lower in the friction typical of in-person relationships, and entirely absent of touch.

“Humans are hard,” says Lim. “But that’s actually the beauty of relationships as well. We are being challenged, we are being pushed. Our ability to think more diversely, be empathetic are challenged by other humans.”

Anxieties about the decline of social fabric and interaction – particularly for young people – have abounded for decades. Telephones and televisions were derided for their antisocial powers long before the term the “ antisocial century ” was coined by US writer Derek Thompson.

“But there is a sense of feeling unsafe right now, generally, whether it’s political safety around the world, or the lack of community,” says Lim. “It affects the way we see our relationships, the way we relate to people, what we choose to do.”

Lim writes about the “loneliness loop” – a particularly nasty trap for young people – by which experiencing loneliness causes the lonely person to perceive social interaction as more threatening, and so they retreat, reduce their social interaction and in doing so become more lonely.

But there is a bigger, community-wide loop too. We have settled, she writes, into a social disconnection crisis.

In The Lonely Generation, Lim imagines a world where social interaction becomes something like exercise has become today: something we once did as part of daily life, but which now we need to make a concerted effort to schedule in our diaries.

“We already see this,” says Lim. Paid-for services coming on to the market as apps or activities in order to facilitate human interaction and combat loneliness. Lim herself receives “so many” requests to endorse different offerings.

“People are capitalising on that,” she says. “This is not to say that they are not a good thing, but I think that it’s really reflective of the erosion of other kinds of social life that we once had.”

Loneliness, particularly youth loneliness, writes Lim, is a signal. A sign that we need to reassess our social world. “There is an ‘us’ problem here.

“People just go, ‘well, it’s not my responsibility’. But the problem is, actually everyone’s responsible,” she says.

“If everyone says that, then we are going to be living in a world, and raising kids in a world, where healthy social connection is ‘a nice to have’.”

articles.content:
Ryan Anderson says he reached out to Blanchard’s father to offer support after apparent overdose death of Ken Urker

The ex-husband of Gypsy Rose Blanchard has said he was “shocked” by the recent death in Louisiana of her former partner Ken Urker – and that he would be there for Blanchard and her daughter “if she needs me”.

Ryan Anderson made those remarks during an appearance on The Sarah Fraser Show podcast on Friday, providing a noteworthy reaction to the latest chapter involving Blanchard, who achieved an unusual level of celebrity in the US after spending time imprisoned for a role in the murder of her abusive mother in Missouri.

Urker was found dead inside his Lafourche parish, Louisiana , home on Thursday on his 34th birthday in what was reported to the local sheriff’s office as an apparent drug overdose.

A Lafourche sheriff’s office report said Blanchard ’s half-brother and his wife went to Urker’s home, saw him lying unconscious through an outside window, and called authorities. Deputies reported that they then went into the home and – among other things – found syringes and a spoon “next to a brown powdery substance” in a bathroom.

Meanwhile, deputies also reported, Urker was dead in a bed next to a nightstand on which was a syringe and a handgun.

Anderson on Friday told Sarah Fraser that his initial reaction to the news of Urker’s death was one of disbelief.

“I was like, ‘No,’” Anderson, 40, said. “My initial thought was shock, like, ‘Hmm, how’d that happen?’ … Shocked that he passed away.”

He also said “my immediate thought went to” Blanchard, 32, and the one-year-old daughter she had with Urker after her marriage to Anderson.

Anderson conceded to Fraser that “exchanges on the phone and … text messages” that he had with Urker “were never good”. But he said he nonetheless reached out to Blanchard’s father, Rod, after learning of Urker’s death.

“I said … ‘Tell Gypsy I’m sorry,’” Anderson recounted. “Tell her I’m here for her if she needs me.

Though Anderson said he “was always somebody who could make her laugh when she was sad or give her comfort”, he described being unsure whether Blanchard would take him up on his offer to be there for her as a friend “strictly”.

A social media statement from Blanchard on Friday said Urker “endured an unimaginable level of public scrutiny and relentless cyberbullying across social media platforms, including TikTok and Reddit” before his death.

“The cruelty directed toward him was something no human being should have to endure,” Blanchard wrote. “I believe the tremendous weight of that scrutiny and harassment had a profound impact on him, and I hope his passing serves as a reminder that there is a real person behind every screen, every headline, and every comment.”

Separately, in an interview with People published on Friday, Blanchard said she did not know whether Urker’s suspected overdose death was intentional.

Despite Urker’s death being reported to the local sheriff’s office as an evident drug overdose, a sheriff’s office captain said the case remained under investigation as of Friday. Capt Brennan Matherne also said that investigators as of Friday had not discovered “any signs of foul play”.

Blanchard spent eight years in prison after being convicted of second-degree murder in connection with the 2015 stabbing death of her mother, Clauddine “Dee Dee” Blanchard.

Dee Dee Blanchard was found stabbed to death in her home in Springfield, Missouri, in June 2015. Gypsy Rose Blanchard gave her then boyfriend, Nicholas Godejohn, a knife that he used to kill her mother.

Blanchard, who hid in a bathroom during her mother’s slaying, pleaded guilty to second-degree murder. Godejohn, whom Blanchard met online, was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole.

Dee Dee Blanchard’s murder drew widespread attention after it was revealed that she had forced Gypsy Rose to pretend she was seriously ill and undergo unnecessary medical procedures.

Blanchard met Urker while serving her sentence in prison, from which she was released in late December 2023. She said on the We Need to Talk podcast in June that Urker had gotten in touch with her while she was incarcerated after he watched Mommy Dead and Dearest, a 2017 documentary about Gypsy Rose and Dee Dee.

Urker proposed in October 2018. But the pair later ended their engagement – before reuniting in August 2019. They eventually broke up again and spent several years apart.

Then, in 2022, while she was still imprisoned, Blanchard married Anderson. She memorably spoke about her marriage to Anderson on the ABC News show 20/20 in January 2024, after her prison release – and defended her public boasting about the intimate satisfaction her then husband provided her.

Blanchard announced that she had separated from Anderson about two months after that interview.

Blanchard and Urker rekindled their relationship in April 2024. Eight months later, they welcomed their daughter, Aurora, in late December 2024.

“Ken was an amazing father and a man who was deeply loved,” Blanchard wrote in her social media statement on Friday. “He will forever be my soulmate and my red string, a connection that time, distance and even death can never erase.”

articles.title: ‘Brave from the beginning’: 20 years of Friday Night Lights – the sports drama that dared to be different
articles.summary: It launched the careers of Jesse Plemons and Michael B Jordan, and let its stars improvise in a way that was fresh and new. Friday Night Lights, which was first broadcast 20 years ago, is set in the most fervent edges of that world, smalltown Texas, where what happens under the floodlights at the end of the working week defines the mood of the place for days to come. It launched the careers of Jesse Plemons and Michael B Jordan, and let its stars improvise in a way that was fresh and new. This show about smalltown US football was confident, trailblazing – and wonderful

I ’ve been around the south of the US enough to have seen the importance of football: little burgs where the high-school football field has stands that wouldn’t disgrace a League Two soccer club in the UK. Friday Night Lights, which was first broadcast 20 years ago, is set in the most fervent edges of that world, smalltown Texas, where what happens under the floodlights at the end of the working week defines the mood of the place for days to come.

Britt Daniel, the frontman of the Texas band Spoon, grew up in one such town, Temple. “Friday Night Lights is based on Odessa, and Odessa and Temple are very, very similar,” he told me in 2017. “The high schools used to play each other at football, and they’re the kind of towns where everything happens on Friday because it’s the football game. I didn’t really think about it until many years later, but you really risked being beaten [up]. Not just harassed, but beaten. Everywhere you went, you really had to look over your shoulder. If you were at the mall, if you were at the parking lot, if you were at a party – people really wanted to fight.”

That was the world into which the Pulitzer-winning reporter HG “Buzz” Bissinger inserted himself. In 1988, he moved to Odessa with his family to write a book about smalltown football. He expected something folksier than he ended up with, which was a portrait of young men being simultaneously revved up like boxers and told to be gentle like priests, all the while burdened with the expectations of their whole community and the pressure to win college scholarships.

It was also a portrait of a town riven with racism, where football sucked precious resources from classroom budgets, and where evidence was everywhere that football was a broken dream, especially in the former golden boys, with their state championship rings, still hanging around Odessa rather than lighting up the NFL.

The book came out in 1990 and was acclaimed everywhere except Odessa. In 1993, it inspired a TV series, Against the Grain, that lasted a single series, and propelled the young Ben Affleck nowhere. There was a 2004 movie that stuck more closely to the book, and was pretty good. And then there was the 2006 series – created by the director of the movie, Peter Berg – which used the book as a starting point for something wonderful: Friday Night Lights.

Odessa became Dillon, home of the Dillon Panthers. In came characters, some clearly based on their counterparts in the book, others entirely new. Out went some of Bissinger’s more troubling reporting, but the thrust of his discomfort with much of life in Odessa was reflected in Dillon.

Friday Night Lights ended up being so good that it transcended difficulties, some of its own making, that might have killed it. Its second season was cut short by a writers’ strike, but was also hampered by melodramatic plotlines. After that second season, with ratings low despite critical acclaim, NBC planned to scrap the show before coming to a co-production deal that saw it air first on cable for the remaining three seasons. It was so good it was possible to forgive its fairytale elements – the show’s de facto hero, coach Eric Taylor (Kyle Chandler), moving to a school across town with no money and no football programme, and making them state champions inside two seasons.

Eric and his wife Tami (Connie Britton, in the role of her lifetime – as was Chandler), a part-time counsellor who somehow becomes principal of Dillon High, are the moral heart of the show, he stern and hard but loyal and trusting, she softer and more empathetic but just as determined. They row, sometimes very badly; they struggle with bringing up their deeply irritating teenage daughter; they live with the insecurity that comes with being a coach at a school with high expectations, and the constant attention and demands it brings.

The show was brave from the beginning. The pilot episode introduced us to the square-jawed leader, the quarterback Jason Street, and his sparkly toothed cheerleader girlfriend Lyla Garrity, our leading man and lady, surely. By the end of the episode, his back was broken. No more football, all hopes and dreams and expectations gone.

The breakout star of the show was supposed to be Taylor Kitsch, playing brooding, handsome, drunken, violent, womanising Tim Riggins, in the vein of James Dean at his most sullen, so puppyish you could forgive him anything, even if Coach couldn’t. He’s the one who went straight to starring roles, but the real winner was the potato-ish actor playing an initially incidental character called Landry Clarke, who grew more central as the series progressed: that was Jesse Plemons , perfect as a teenager who’s clever but knows that is rarely an advantage and often a disadvantage in this world, especially when paired with a lack of the only thing that is respected: physical prowess. (Landry’s hapless and hopeless alt-rock band is just the perfect thing for his character.)

A more likely star emerged in Michael B Jordan , making the transition from child soap player to dramatic actor as the quarterback Vince Howard in the final two series (his flirtation with Jurnee Smollett’s Jess Merriweather is one of the show’s most touching relationships).

Berg encouraged his cast to improvise, had scenes filmed with handheld cameras and did away with “blocking” – the discipline of telling actors exactly where to move throughout a scene. As long as story beats were met, they could adapt dialogue and reactions. It gave the show a naturalism that felt new and fresh in a network drama: when characters paused to think of a reply, they were actually thinking, not just pausing.

The female characters had lives of their own and weren’t simply adjuncts to the football (Britton had played coach Billy Bob Thornton’s wife in the movie, and had not been willing to return only to reprise looking pretty in the corner). Admittedly, except for quarterback Matt Saracen’s dementia-ridden grandma, they were all stunningly beautiful, but then so were pretty much all the men. Berg’s camera, though, had a covetous eye for its young cast, male and female alike: it’s hard not to look great through a filter against a Texas sunset, as Kitsch was so often shown, often muttering, “Texas f’rever.”

Friday Night Lights didn’t overstay its welcome: 76 episodes over five seasons. At times it creaked, but its humanity always tethered it, and its sense of place was constant. If Buffy the Vampire Slayer’s Sunnydale was hilarious because it would just invent locations – here are some docks! Here’s an airport! – Dillon was the opposite. It had nothing. Fast food, a bar, a car dealership, and the open range. All it had was football, and the Friday night lights. Just like Odessa and Temple, towns where anything could go wrong.

articles.content:
Her last novel sold 5m copies and was adapted into a hit series. Nearly 10 years on, the Korean-American author has written another epic. She discusses ambition and the diagnosis that inspired her to leave work and write

B ack in 1995, when she was in her mid-20s, Min Jin Lee quit her job as a corporate lawyer. As a teenager she had been diagnosed as a hepatitis B carrier and doctors told her she was highly likely to develop liver cancer in her 20s or 30s. “I thought, if I’m going to die, I’m going to write a book first,” the now 57-year-old Korean-American author says of her decision to turn her back on a regular pay cheque and healthcare. “I was told so many times that I was going to get sicker and sicker, that I’ve always felt that if I can get a really good book out then I’m done.”

Lee, looking very much alive and well, is on a video call from her home in Harlem, New York, floor-to-ceiling bookshelves behind her. We are meeting to discuss the publication of her third novel, American Hagwon, the final part in what she calls her “Korean trilogy”, following Free Food for Millionaires in 2007 and her 2017 international bestseller, Pachinko , stylishly adapted for Apple TV in 2022. “Korean quartet!” she corrects me now. Thanks to experimental drugs, she is now so healthy she can commit to another book. “Before I turn 70, I should turn in my manuscript,” she jokes. “I’m writing the four books that I wanted to write and after that I’m going to take a long nap.”

Lee averages a book a decade. It took 11 years of writing before Free Food for Millionaires, about the children of Korean immigrants in New York in the 90s, was published. She worked on Pachinko, which spans nearly a century, and ranges from a fishing village in Japanese-occupied Korea to Wall Street in the 1980s, for 20 years. It was voted one of the New York Times 100 best books of the century and has sold more than 5m globally. American Hagwon, which follows one family from Seoul to Sydney to California in the years leading up to and after the Asian financial crisis of 1997, was bought in a 12-way publishing auction. She has recently returned from Germany on a research trip for her next book, her “European novel”, which already has a title: Marshall Plan. Its starting point is the 1963 bilateral agreement when thousands of Koreans were sent to West Germany to work as miners or nurses to boost the economy back home. The only thing all four novels have in common is the Korean diaspora.

“I’ve had to have lessons to do this, to talk to you,” Lee confesses, smiling into the screen. A once desperately shy and poor girl from Seoul, she is both modest about her success – “I’m used to feeling unwanted” – and proud that she has pulled it off. “Wow, I have done this. I have fucking done this. I would love to know how many Asian American women have been published in the New York Review of Books,” Lee told the Believer Magazine. Her NYRB essay was an indepth appraisal of the work of fellow novelist Han Kang, who became the first Korean Nobel prize for literature laureate in 2024. While Lee’s sprawling multi­generational epics couldn’t be more different from Han’s slim, poetic novels, they both tackle periods of their country’s troubled history that the world has chosen to forget. Ironically, they have come to prominence on the crest of hallyu, the Korean Wave, the government-sponsored cultural push that has given the west K-pop bands and Squid Game.

Each weighing in at more than 500 pages, Lee’s novels take up as much space on a bookshelf as the life’s work of other writers. “I would love to write a short novel, but I don’t know how with these subjects,” she says. “I always think: ‘God, pick something easier. What is the matter with you? How about two people having feelings at a kitchen table?’”

As big-hearted as they are physically hefty, her books have the immersive narrative drive, social conscience and moral purpose of the Victorian classics, on which she trained herself as a writer. “Almost all the people that I admire the most in terms of writers are old dead British writers,” she says. “Austen and Eliot, they have enormous hearts, they’re so romantic in terms of what they think human beings can be.”

If her first two novels dealt with assimilation and colonisation, respectively, American Hagwon takes on one of the most important things to Koreans around the world: education. “Hagwon” is the term for private cram schools that are ubiquitous in South Korea . “If there was one word that I wanted you to know, that it’s so important for you to understand any Korean person you’ll ever meet, it’s ‘hagwon’,” Lee says. “In Korea that word is almost like the word water.” Some publishers were uneasy with Pachinko as a title, because it was unfamiliar to western readers. But this noisy pinball machine found in pachinko parlours across Korea was the perfect metaphor for the unpredictability of success, especially when the odds are stacked against you, as they were for the Korean-Japanese immigrants.

In American Hagwon, John and Helen Koh are forced to uproot their family after a business betrayal: John swaps a well-paid job in insurance to manage a nail bar in LA, and their three children – Bo, DH and Mido – have to learn harder lessons than those taught in any classroom. More than 600 pages devoted to studying, tutoring and the establishment of a hagwon business, a concept unfamiliar to most readers outside Korea, might be a tough sell. But American Hagwon is about much more than swotting for exams. Lee wants to show the true cost of the overachieving Asian stereotype, the sacrifices of the “tiger mom” and the inequities of the elite education system. “How do you live a wise life?” the novel asks. It is a story of “power and ambition and getting to your goals”, she says. “In America, we really worship work but we also really worship success. We don’t always worship how people get there. In Korea, people really do examine how you get there.”

She likes to set out her thesis in the opening line of each of her novels: “Competence can be a curse” in Free Food for Millionaires; “History has failed us, but no matter” in Pachinko. “The rules of engagement have changed already,” she declares at the start of American Hagwon. “There was a time when we felt we could sort of predict things,” she says now. “But right now most people are feeling: ‘I have no idea what just happened, no idea what will happen. I don’t know how to raise my children or plan my career because shit just keeps happening. And the people who are changing the rules aren’t sending us memos.’ I think that is where advanced economies are right now. Of course,” she adds, “people who are not from advanced economies have always felt this way.”

All her novels take the Asian immigrant experience from the margins to the mainstream. “In my pages, I want to be the centre,” as she puts it. But she is also reflecting our global contemporary predicament. Diaspora “is a permanent condition for every single person in the world,” she says. “Now we have economic diaspora and we also have environmental diaspora. The people that I focus on are obviously Koreans, but what I’m really writing about is when you have to leave because you’re no longer useful or you’re no longer wanted, what do you do? You have to adapt.”

Lee’s own story has the epic sweep of her novels. Her father was a war refugee who fled North Korea when he was 16, never to see his family again. He met her mother, a piano teacher, in Seoul. The family moved to the US when Min was seven, where they lived in an apartment in Elmhurst, Queens. The middle of three sisters, she remembers it as an “ugly little hovel”, with mice and bugs. Her father bought a newsstand, where the young Min would sit on the weekends. After a year, they bought a wholesale jewellers, not much bigger than the newspaper kiosk, selling costume jewellery to street pedlars. Both her parents worked in the shop six days a week. Her father is now 91, her mother 86, and she visits them in New Jersey after church each Sunday.

“I didn’t have any friends and I really couldn’t get on,” she says of her own school days. Things improved when she got into Bronx High School of Science (also attended by NYC mayor Zohran Mamdani). But she felt out of her depth once again at Yale, where “there were so few Asians and everybody was so much wealthier”. Her two years as a lawyer, condensing boxes of documents into 20-page memos, proved a perfect training for a novelist intent on taking on huge hunks of Korean history. She married her husband, Christopher Duffy, who is half Japanese and half European, when she was 24, and their son was born when she was 29. “I really did think I was going to die,” she says. “I thought I had to get everything done.”

Walking home from the subway one day after reading VS Naipaul’s A House for Mr Biswas , she realised that here was her subject. “I had to write about the disgraced, the poor and the earnest strivers of Queens,” she wrote in an essay in the New York Times. She took classes at Harvard Business School and a whole semester in millinery at a fashion college as research for Free Food for Millionaires.

In 2007, the year it was finally published, Duffy was relocated to Tokyo. The seed for Pachinko had been sown 20 years earlier at Yale, when she attended a lecture by a visiting Japanese missionary about a Korean immigrant boy in Japan who killed himself because he was bullied. She had a draft of a novel, entitled Motherland, but it was too “dry” and “angry”. Living in Tokyo and talking to hundreds of Korean immigrants – street sellers, security guards, Uber drivers – Pachniko came to life. “Literary fiction must incorporate those stories,” she says. “Writing about work is something that social novelists must do.”

It is no surprise that these epic novels about ordinary people at the mercy of cataclysmic social and economic changes have struck a chord right now. “The thing that I’ve always been able to do is to listen. And I’m willing to listen if someone will tell me how difficult their lives are,” she says. But she also wants to capture the resilience and joy of the people she speaks to. “There’s a wish for more love and recognition that regular human beings have and also a kind of buoyancy,” she says. “You read the dismal horrible stuff, but then we still have sex and have children. How do I connect that? The way I see it is because we adapt and we have humour.”

She has no truck with the vogue for autofiction – “It’s for a certain reader. I’m probably not her” – which she feels has no place for the people she writes about. Having been on judging panels for many book prizes in the US, she has come to the conclusion that she doesn’t fit in with other contemporary writers. “My peers are writing wonderful, incredibly moving things, but I don’t know how to write like that.”

She survived her wilderness years by following American author Grace Paley’s advice to writers to “keep a low overhead”, and also by having “a low overhead for expectations of recognition”. Today, she still leads a very quiet life. “I’m not a cool literary It person,” she says. “But I get to do what I want to do.” Her working day begins by reading and making notes on a chapter of the Bible, which Willa Cather used to do before writing. She diagrams everything – character outlines, plot – and looks for gaps. When she has a first draft she is happy with, she throws it away. Her manuscripts push 200,000 words. “I’ll just start all over,” she says, breezily. “It’s so much cleaner when you do it that way.”

It is only since the success of the Pachinko TV series (on which she is remaining tight-lipped, after withdrawing as an executive producer) that she feels part of the publishing scene. “It’s like I’m visiting. I feel like, they’re letting me come and I’ll behave myself and I’ll be on time, but if I’m not asked again, I will just be grateful for the opportunity.” But there is nothing modest about her literary ambitions. “I want to build a palace,” she says of her novels. “I want to build a palace that stands.”

In return for the commitment of their time, she wants the reader to feel changed by the experience, just as she has been by reading 19th-century novels. “I probably feel more British than anything because I’ve read so much British literature, over and over again,” she says. “That is what I am trying to do, in some ways. I’m trying to make you Korean.”

American Hagwon by Min Jin Lee is published by 4th Estate. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com . Delivery charges may apply.

Each weighing in at more than 500 pages, Lee’s novels take up as much space on a bookshelf as the life’s work of other writers. “I would love to write a short novel, but I don’t know how with these subjects,” she says. “I always think: ‘God, pick something easier. What is the matter with you? How about two people having feelings at a kitchen table?’”

As big-hearted as they are physically hefty, her books have the immersive narrative drive, social conscience and moral purpose of the Victorian classics, on which she trained herself as a writer. “Almost all the people that I admire the most in terms of writers are old dead British writers,” she says. “Austen and Eliot, they have enormous hearts, they’re so romantic in terms of what they think human beings can be.”

If her first two novels dealt with assimilation and colonisation, respectively, American Hagwon takes on one of the most important things to Koreans around the world: education. “Hagwon” is the term for private cram schools that are ubiquitous in South Korea . “If there was one word that I wanted you to know, that it’s so important for you to understand any Korean person you’ll ever meet, it’s ‘hagwon’,” Lee says. “In Korea that word is almost like the word water.” Some publishers were uneasy with Pachinko as a title, because it was unfamiliar to western readers. But this noisy pinball machine found in pachinko parlours across Korea was the perfect metaphor for the unpredictability of success, especially when the odds are stacked against you, as they were for the Korean-Japanese immigrants.

In American Hagwon, John and Helen Koh are forced to uproot their family after a business betrayal: John swaps a well-paid job in insurance to manage a nail bar in LA, and their three children – Bo, DH and Mido – have to learn harder lessons than those taught in any classroom. More than 600 pages devoted to studying, tutoring and the establishment of a hagwon business, a concept unfamiliar to most readers outside Korea, might be a tough sell. But American Hagwon is about much more than swotting for exams. Lee wants to show the true cost of the overachieving Asian stereotype, the sacrifices of the “tiger mom” and the inequities of the elite education system. “How do you live a wise life?” the novel asks. It is a story of “power and ambition and getting to your goals”, she says. “In America, we really worship work but we also really worship success. We don’t always worship how people get there. In Korea, people really do examine how you get there.”

She likes to set out her thesis in the opening line of each of her novels: “Competence can be a curse” in Free Food for Millionaires; “History has failed us, but no matter” in Pachinko. “The rules of engagement have changed already,” she declares at the start of American Hagwon. “There was a time when we felt we could sort of predict things,” she says now. “But right now most people are feeling: ‘I have no idea what just happened, no idea what will happen. I don’t know how to raise my children or plan my career because shit just keeps happening. And the people who are changing the rules aren’t sending us memos.’ I think that is where advanced economies are right now. Of course,” she adds, “people who are not from advanced economies have always felt this way.”

All her novels take the Asian immigrant experience from the margins to the mainstream. “In my pages, I want to be the centre,” as she puts it. But she is also reflecting our global contemporary predicament. Diaspora “is a permanent condition for every single person in the world,” she says. “Now we have economic diaspora and we also have environmental diaspora. The people that I focus on are obviously Koreans, but what I’m really writing about is when you have to leave because you’re no longer useful or you’re no longer wanted, what do you do? You have to adapt.”

Lee’s own story has the epic sweep of her novels. Her father was a war refugee who fled North Korea when he was 16, never to see his family again. He met her mother, a piano teacher, in Seoul. The family moved to the US when Min was seven, where they lived in an apartment in Elmhurst, Queens. The middle of three sisters, she remembers it as an “ugly little hovel”, with mice and bugs. Her father bought a newsstand, where the young Min would sit on the weekends. After a year, they bought a wholesale jewellers, not much bigger than the newspaper kiosk, selling costume jewellery to street pedlars. Both her parents worked in the shop six days a week. Her father is now 91, her mother 86, and she visits them in New Jersey after church each Sunday.

“I didn’t have any friends and I really couldn’t get on,” she says of her own school days. Things improved when she got into Bronx High School of Science (also attended by NYC mayor Zohran Mamdani). But she felt out of her depth once again at Yale, where “there were so few Asians and everybody was so much wealthier”. Her two years as a lawyer, condensing boxes of documents into 20-page memos, proved a perfect training for a novelist intent on taking on huge hunks of Korean history. She married her husband, Christopher Duffy, who is half Japanese and half European, when she was 24, and their son was born when she was 29. “I really did think I was going to die,” she says. “I thought I had to get everything done.”

Walking home from the subway one day after reading VS Naipaul’s A House for Mr Biswas , she realised that here was her subject. “I had to write about the disgraced, the poor and the earnest strivers of Queens,” she wrote in an essay in the New York Times. She took classes at Harvard Business School and a whole semester in millinery at a fashion college as research for Free Food for Millionaires.

In 2007, the year it was finally published, Duffy was relocated to Tokyo. The seed for Pachinko had been sown 20 years earlier at Yale, when she attended a lecture by a visiting Japanese missionary about a Korean immigrant boy in Japan who killed himself because he was bullied. She had a draft of a novel, entitled Motherland, but it was too “dry” and “angry”. Living in Tokyo and talking to hundreds of Korean immigrants – street sellers, security guards, Uber drivers – Pachniko came to life. “Literary fiction must incorporate those stories,” she says. “Writing about work is something that social novelists must do.”

It is no surprise that these epic novels about ordinary people at the mercy of cataclysmic social and economic changes have struck a chord right now. “The thing that I’ve always been able to do is to listen. And I’m willing to listen if someone will tell me how difficult their lives are,” she says. But she also wants to capture the resilience and joy of the people she speaks to. “There’s a wish for more love and recognition that regular human beings have and also a kind of buoyancy,” she says. “You read the dismal horrible stuff, but then we still have sex and have children. How do I connect that? The way I see it is because we adapt and we have humour.”

She has no truck with the vogue for autofiction – “It’s for a certain reader. I’m probably not her” – which she feels has no place for the people she writes about. Having been on judging panels for many book prizes in the US, she has come to the conclusion that she doesn’t fit in with other contemporary writers. “My peers are writing wonderful, incredibly moving things, but I don’t know how to write like that.”

She survived her wilderness years by following American author Grace Paley’s advice to writers to “keep a low overhead”, and also by having “a low overhead for expectations of recognition”. Today, she still leads a very quiet life. “I’m not a cool literary It person,” she says. “But I get to do what I want to do.” Her working day begins by reading and making notes on a chapter of the Bible, which Willa Cather used to do before writing. She diagrams everything – character outlines, plot – and looks for gaps. When she has a first draft she is happy with, she throws it away. Her manuscripts push 200,000 words. “I’ll just start all over,” she says, breezily. “It’s so much cleaner when you do it that way.”

It is only since the success of the Pachinko TV series (on which she is remaining tight-lipped, after withdrawing as an executive producer) that she feels part of the publishing scene. “It’s like I’m visiting. I feel like, they’re letting me come and I’ll behave myself and I’ll be on time, but if I’m not asked again, I will just be grateful for the opportunity.” But there is nothing modest about her literary ambitions. “I want to build a palace,” she says of her novels. “I want to build a palace that stands.”

In return for the commitment of their time, she wants the reader to feel changed by the experience, just as she has been by reading 19th-century novels. “I probably feel more British than anything because I’ve read so much British literature, over and over again,” she says. “That is what I am trying to do, in some ways. I’m trying to make you Korean.”
American Hagwon by Min Jin Lee is published by 4th Estate. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com . Delivery charges may apply.

articles.title: They’re delicious, popular and versatile – but how healthy are berries?

articles.content:
Experts say that if you’re eating any berry – strawberries, blackberries, currants, raspberries, blueberries – you are benefiting

Sprinkled on top of yoghurt, blended into smoothies or baked into crumbles, berries are among Americans’ favorite fruits.

Luckily, berries are as healthy as they are delicious and versatile: low in calories, full of vitamins and antioxidants, and a good source of fiber. Research shows that, depending on the type, berries support cardiovascular health , may boost gut health and fight inflammation and show promise as part of a “healthy dietary strategy for diabetes prevention and management”, to quote researchers . Meta-analyses also link compounds in berries with improved cognitive health.

Polyphenols are a broad category of plant compounds; in berries, the most active and proportionally meaningful of them are anthocyanins, which also give many berries their blue, purple and red pigments.

Researchers are investigating whether berry polyphenols and the metabolites produced when gut microbes process them may influence inflammation and blood-vessel function. Because the brain depends on an extensive blood supply, better vascular function is one plausible route by which berries could support cognition.

“In simple terms, the anthocyanins are likely creating a healthy working environment for brain cells by improving blood flow into the brain, which improves oxygenation and nutrient delivery,” said Tim Crowe, a nutrition scientist who closely follows anthocyanin research. “What’s good for our blood vessels is also good for our brain.”

The equivalent of a daily cup of blueberries was linked to slightly improved speed of information processing relative to a placebo in older adults with mild cognitive impairment over a six-month period, according to research by Mary Ann Lila, a professor in the department of food, bioprocessing, and nutrition sciences at North Carolina State University. That suggests berries could not only be neuro-protective, but an intervention for those already experiencing cognitive decline. “A pretty amazing result,” said Lila.

A particular pattern of eating called the Mind diet – a version of the Mediterranean diet geared toward supporting cognitive health – involves berries. “We have a strong indication that diets that are higher in berries over many years tend to have slower cognitive decline and delaying of cognitive ageing,” said Moon, who has written a book about the Mind diet.

In the 2015 study informing the Mind diet, researchers observed 923 participants. They found those who prioritized whole foods including berries, leafy greens , nuts and seeds, beans , fatty fish and olive oil – while avoiding sweets, ultra-processed foods and red meat – for an average of 4.5 years had a 53% lower risk of developing Alzheimer’s compared with those who did not.

Experts say that if you’re eating any berry – strawberries, blackberries, currants, raspberries, blueberries – you’re benefiting.

“All berries are good. We should eat a heck of a lot more than we do,” said Lila.

However, some studies suggest wild berries may have a bit of a nutritional leg up on their conventionally grown counterparts, because they develop an “abundance of phytochemical resources” to “defend them against the environment”, Lila said. “Those are the same phytochemicals that when we consume them … dispel human chronic diseases.”

Each type of berry has its own valuable nutritional fingerprint. Some punch above their weight in particular categories. For instance, cranberries are the only commercially cultivated berry with a significant amount of “a particular kind of polyphenol called an A-type proanthocyanidin” which helps prevent recurrent urinary tract infections, said Lila.

Blackcurrants, meanwhile, provide the most vitamin C per cup of raw berries – about 190mg, compared with only 15mg in blueberries. Raspberries are fiber champions, with 8g, or about a third of your daily fiber needs, per cup.

Blueberries contain high levels of anthocyanins, and are colloquially lauded as a superfood – but that doesn’t necessarily mean that blue is best. Other varieties could have similar benefits, but blueberries are “the well-studied one” because they are known to produce positive findings in nutrition research studies, said Crowe.

Moon recommends eating a cup of berries a day, though she notes that any amount you add to your diet regularly is a net positive. “The more people are eating fruits and vegetables, including berries, the better,” she said.

Berries usually appear on the Dirty Dozen , an annual list made by the non-profit Environmental Working Group. The EWG tests produce for pesticide residue and the results often make headlines, causing people to wonder whether they should be avoiding certain fruits and vegetables.

It is important that pesticide residue on organic and conventional produce remain below the regulatory limits. In the US, these are set by the Environmental Protection Agency, and monitored and enforced by federal regulators such as the Food and Drug Administration and the US Department of Agriculture. But mere detection of a substance doesn’t automatically translate to a dangerous concentration.

“The dose makes the poison, and detection is not the same as harm. The very real benefits of eating a variety of any produce, including berries, outweigh theoretical risks,” said Moon. “No major scientific or public health organization recommends avoiding conventionally grown produce, including berries.”

“You’d need to eat hundreds of servings of each food to even hit the safety threshold, which is already 100-1,000 times lower than a level that could theoretically cause harm,” writes science communicator, microbiologist and immunologist Dr Andrea Love in her 2025 assessment of the Dirty Dozen.

“Fresh and frozen berries have fairly similar nutrient profiles,” said Moon. Frozen berries are flash-frozen soon after being harvested, meaning they retain their nutrients well. Frozen berries are convenient and potentially cheaper than fresh ones, added Crowe. Freeze-dried berries also retain their nutrients.

However, anthocyanins are heat-sensitive, and research has found that they can be reduced in berries by up to 80% in prolonged, high-heat processes such as jam-making.

Berries aren’t just for breakfast or sweet preparations, either. “One of my favorite ways to eat berries is a wild berry salsa – all the ingredients of a salsa minus the tomatoes, with wild blueberries standing in,” said Lila. “It’s a beautiful blue, cold dish you scoop up with chips, and since it’s raw, you’re not losing any potency to heat.”
