articles.content:
Sixty top architecture firms from around the world have mooted 500 eye-catching projects across Albania, sparking fury and protests. Now they’re being celebrated in an 800-page tome that some are calling ‘a smoking gun’

L ast autumn, I was sitting with a prominent architect in New York, when their phone wouldn’t stop buzzing. They finally checked the messages and chuckled. “Oh, the Albanian Architecture Army chat is blowing up again,” they said. “It looks like Edi has some new projects for us.”

Edi was Edi Rama, the prime minister of Albania since 2013, who has been presiding over the rapid transformation of the former communist country with a fleet of glamorous building projects. There are twisting towers in Tirana, along with prize-winning public spaces , striking coastal resorts, and many more dazzling visions on the way – all now brought together in a hefty new book, The Albanian Files .

The country’s makeover, it turns out, is partly coordinated via a WhatsApp group (“Albanian ArchArmy” for short) which includes some of the most famous architects in the world. It is a forum where achievements are shared, new projects celebrated, and the great prime minister-patron showered with praise for his bravery and boldness. The New York architect describes the situation in the manner of a superhero movie: Rama sends out the signal and the world’s starchitects rally to the rescue with their daring designs. Look hard enough and you might even see the Albanian double-headed eagle projected into the night sky.

The WhatsApp chat might be confidential, but The Albanian Files is the next best thing. It is a remarkable document, in ways that are both intended and not. In his foreword, Rama describes the book as “a precious behind-the-scenes record” of a process that is “lifting Albania in a way that nobody saw coming”. It is an eye-opening directory of dreams, in which 60 international practices (and not a single Albanian one) lay out their plans for over 500 projects up and down the country.

To Rama’s critics, however, the book is an 800-page, 2.2kg dossier of evidence. They point to the opacity of decision-making , the destruction of heritage , the forced evictions , the trampling of protected landscapes , and the role of Albania’s construction industry in laundering money for organised crime . The publication is full of first-hand testimonies by architects documenting their experiences, and one opposition MP has called it the “smoking gun” – although there is no suggestion that the architects have been involved in any wrongdoing. Rama is right that nobody saw it coming: most of the projects in the book’s pages are news to the local population, which has reacted with fury.

“Starchitects go home!” read one placard at a noisy protest in June , outside a venue in Tirana, where many of the architects in the book were gathered for an exclusive event to celebrate their work and launch the publication. “Where is the public?” read another. Tickets for the architecture festival, titled Landscapes of Abundance , cost up to €200, in a country where the median monthly wage is €700. It came at a charged moment, just a few weeks after huge national protests were ignited by the multibillion dollar plans to develop Zvërnec nature reserve and the nearby island of Sazan into a luxury resort , backed by the Trump family.

Dubbed the flamingo revolution , in reference to the fragile habitats critics say will be trampled by the project, the protests have now continued for over 120 days, with ever-louder calls for Rama’s resignation. Architecture has found itself unexpectedly in the firing line.

“It feels like living in an autocratic kingdom,” says Lorin Kadiu, director of Citizens.al , an investigative news platform that has been tracking construction projects in Albania since 2018. “Not just the lack of transparency, but the fact that we must all be subjected to the aesthetic tastes of one person. The whole country must be painted the way he wants.”

Rama, who trained as a painter, first rose to prominence as the mayor of Tirana in the 2000s, when he made international headlines with his programme of painting the dreary soviet blocks a rainbow of jaunty colours . The cheap and cheerful makeover worked, and Rama was hailed for his maverick artistic approach.

But, now, many of his former supporters feel like his architectural ambitions have gone too far. An open letter , handed out at the protests, denounced the “art-washing of bulldozer politics,” and asked the assembled architects if they enjoy “the freedom to do here what would be forbidden, challenged, or otherwise made impossible in your own countries?” Of the architects contacted by the Guardian, only one responded, to say they do not do anything in Albania that they would not be allowed to do in another place. They added that “the freedom in Albania is certainly alluring and as such the personal responsibility is greater”.

As Rama writes pointedly in his foreword to The Albanian Files, the architects are attracted to work in Albania by the “freedom from ‘no’ in all its forms”. The pages are studded with visions for virgin coastlines, verdant forests, and pristine dunes and lagoons. In Gjipe, a bay that many consider the last virgin beach in southern Albania, Dutch firm MVRDV has proposed a mirrored glass hotel that would span the gorge , “like a jewel on the coastline”.

It comes hot on the heels of their apartment tower in Tirana shaped like the head of Skanderbeg , Albania’s national hero (which also bears a striking resemblance to Rama). In the protected dune area of Rana e Hedhun, the venerable Portuguese architect Álvaro Siza has masterplanned a hillside development with a cable car and a tower-block on the beach .

A few pages later, Swiss maestro Valerio Olgiati proposes a cluster of concrete towers rising from the sand, peppered with defensive windows . It looks as if he might be preparing to fend off an invasion from the sea.

The coastal glow-up continues with the Florentine luxury yacht designer Luca Dini (studio mission: “to astonish even the most discerning”). He presents an illustrated voyage through his 17 projects, including the Life Marina Complex, spanning seven kilometres of virgin coastline near Saranda, and the Atara resort, with a golden “crown” that hovers above the cliffs like another military lookout post. It almost reaches parody when his comic-style illustrations conclude with an image of a super-yacht hurtling above a skyline, with the designer himself declaiming from the deck: “[we] create spaces that harmonise with the environment.”

The book’s editor, Anneke Abhelakh, asked the architects to submit their own texts, and they are striking in their honesty. At times it reads like a hot-mic transcript. “Because there are not many rules and my clients care very little for the context,” writes Berlin-based architect Sam Chermayeff, “we are forced to think through our own values.” He recounts the “truly wild” experience of working in Albania, including how he was called, out of the blue, by one of Rama’s associates, and soon asked to design two towers in Tirana , totalling 45,000sq m – quite something for a designer better known for experimental kitchens.

“Of course I agreed,” he adds, “not really understanding what was happening.” Contacted for comment, Chermayeff responded: “I do ask Albanian clients the same questions that I ask of clients in any country and am equally assured,” adding that “as in Germany or the US, I really do not know more than what I am told,” and that he does not work in or near protected areas. “I do not do anything,” he added, “I would not do at another place.”

Austrian architect Chris Precht describes how he was approached on Instagram by Rama himself, “asking if I would be interested in working in Albania”. He now has 29 projects to his name, including a €4m “ Garden of Eden ”, built in the courtyard of the prime minister’s own office.

“It is an unimaginable reality,” says a campaign group of Albanian architects and urban planners, Arkitektët Shqiparë , which has created an online database of all of the projects – published in Albanian, unlike the book. “A narrow group of foreign architects is contacted directly by the prime minister’s office and receives projects without a competitive procedure.”

articles.content:
Film-makers Laura Poitras and Rachel Lauren Mueller’s new short is an unvarnished portrait of ICE-occupied Minneapolis

Get Out . The Texas Chainsaw Massacre . The Purge . All three films build on an august tradition of using horror as a Trojan horse to comment on the social, political and racial anxieties of their day. They’re Here, a new documentary featured in this year’s New York film festival , flips the script. Directed by Rachel Lauren Mueller , a film-maker and journalist, and Laura Poitras , Academy award-winner, the 24-minute film employs horror tropes to re-examine the surge of Immigration and Customs Enforcement ( ICE ) officers in Minneapolis last winter. “For film-makers and journalists, there’s a great sense of responsibility in these moments when they arise,” said Mueller, a Minneapolis resident. “This is my neighborhood. It was my community. It was very clear to me what my role in this moment would be.”

Framed as a dystopian story set in an urban tundra, They’re Here follows the Trump administration’s border control campaign in Minnesota – officially dubbed Operation Metro Surge . Over the course of three winter months, the Department of Homeland Security moved to remove the Twin Cities’ Somali immigrant population and destabilize its progressive political order. The documentary takes in the wanton shock-and-awe campaign and scales it down to the battlefield, following Minneapolis residents as they evade and resist ICE and Customs and Border Protection agents – obscuring the residents’ identities for protection.

It opens on an overcast, -10F (-23C) day with one woman who goes by the pseudonym “Liz Lemon” on a conference call with other vigilant members of her community as she follows an ICE detail patrolling her neighborhood. When the agents make as if to leave, only to lead her back to her own front door and point at it, she fumes: “Are you pointing to my house like I don’t know where I live? Fuck off!”

They’re Here’s tapestry of dash-cam video, counter-surveillance and crowdsourced footage from the ground puts viewers in the thick of the anxious moment. The directors say their film and its tone were inspired by a 10-second Instagram post of a winter’s drive through the woods, overlaid with a soundtrack that rivaled Prince in its resonance across the Twin Cities – replete with honking horns, whistles and cries to “close your doors” as balaclava-shrouded ICE and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agents crash into their daily routines. The film’s title borrows from another citizen callout – the most resigned of them all, perhaps. “One of the things we’re trying to do with this film is put the audience in a position of terror and fear,” said Poitras.

They’re Here doesn’t just chronicle the disruptions to quotidian life – an apartment view of a quiet intersection suddenly turned into a chaotic backdrop by federal agents in gas masks firing smoke bombs to clear the streets after the killing of Alex Pretti by federal agents. It pushes in on the violence: one agent rag-dolling a female protester to the icy pavement, others pepper-spraying citizens right in the eyes. It captures Greg Bovino , the notable federal law enforcement officer in this hellish tableau whose face wasn’t obscured, charging into a crowd of protesters and backing down one guy shielding himself with his bike. “You hit me with that bike, you’re done,” the former ICE majordomo snarls.

Even more stunning than the scene is the source of that footage: a pair of Chicago teenagers who had been tracking the national ICE crackdown independently. “I didn’t know them at the time, but we were all at that moment together,” said Mueller, reflecting on a film-making responsibility that morphed from a journalistic call of duty to a personal shield. “There was a moment when I’m out of the car and there was an ICE agent threatening to smash this person’s window, and he’s screaming. I’m maybe 6ft away and my camera, a DSLR, is not small. But the [agent] turned, saw the camera and took a step back – like he was really startled by how big it was. There was a physical barrier with this particular camera, but ICE agents were seeing it in a different light than the rest of the documentation that was happening.”

Just as powerful are the scenes from the Minneapolis-Saint Paul airport – of detainees in the frigid cold, wearing little more than shackles and a prison jumpsuit, being herded on to non-commercial airliners before being secreted off to any number of federal detention centers across the country or deported entirely – as visuals by professional plane watcher Nick Benson and data journalist Josh Begley makes clear. It all unfolds with the understanding that travelers rushing to catch their connecting flights – who aren’t shown – have scant awareness of the horror they’re passing through.

But the heart of the film is Edén Villa, a pseudonymous Latin American immigrant who is seen (but never pictured) and heard as he’s being smuggled to work in the trunk of a car. It’s a risk, sure – but, as he implies, any extended home hideout would depend on a steady job to maintain cover. It’s the kind of personal testimony that breaks Operation Metro Surge out of the news cycle into the realm of art as a historical artifact. “It just grows out of this longstanding belief I’ve had that cinema can help understand moments we’re living in – particularly political moments or moments of crisis, moments of violence, moments of extreme state abuse of power,” said Poitras, who has returned to these themes often in her films on fellow chroniclers Edward Snowden , Julian Assange and the investigative journalist Seymour Hersh . “We have these tools that can get at truth in different types of ways that are emotional.”

And even though the DHS’s recent change in tactics, from shock-and-awe to blending into the background and lying in wait , would seem to suggest that the federal government’s offensive has only evolved, the fact that it was even forced to turn down the temperature gives this horror story satisfying heroes: Minnesota residents who were clearly underestimated as hapless victims. “There’s a history of resistance here that goes back decades,” Mueller said. “Early labor movements started here. The American Indian movement started in the Twin Cities. The resistance that happened in Minneapolis would not have been possible if the networks weren’t in place after the uprising after George Floyd ’s murder. And that uprising wouldn’t have happened if Philando Castile hadn’t been killed. Each one of these pieces builds upon itself.”

They’re Here screened at the New York film festival with UK, Australia and further US screenings to be announced

It captures Greg Bovino , the notable federal law enforcement officer in this hellish tableau whose face wasn’t obscured, charging into a crowd of protesters and backing down one guy shielding himself with his bike. “You hit me with that bike, you’re done,” the former ICE majordomo snarls.

Even more stunning than the scene is the source of that footage: a pair of Chicago teenagers who had been tracking the national ICE crackdown independently. “I didn’t know them at the time, but we were all at that moment together,” said Mueller, reflecting on a film-making responsibility that morphed from a journalistic call of duty to a personal shield. “There was a moment when I’m out of the car and there was an ICE agent threatening to smash this person’s window, and he’s screaming. I’m maybe 6ft away and my camera, a DSLR, is not small. But the [agent] turned, saw the camera and took a step back – like he was really startled by how big it was. There was a physical barrier with this particular camera, but ICE agents were seeing it in a different light than the rest of the documentation that was happening.”

Just as powerful are the scenes from the Minneapolis-Saint Paul airport – of detainees in the frigid cold, wearing little more than shackles and a prison jumpsuit, being herded on to non-commercial airliners before being secreted off to any number of federal detention centers across the country or deported entirely – as visuals by professional plane watcher Nick Benson and data journalist Josh Begley makes clear. It all unfolds with the understanding that travelers rushing to catch their connecting flights – who aren’t shown – have scant awareness of the horror they’re passing through.

But the heart of the film is Edén Villa, a pseudonymous Latin American immigrant who is seen (but never pictured) and heard as he’s being smuggled to work in the trunk of a car. It’s a risk, sure – but, as he implies, any extended home hideout would depend on a steady job to maintain cover. It’s the kind of personal testimony that breaks Operation Metro Surge out of the news cycle into the realm of art as a historical artifact. “It just grows out of this longstanding belief I’ve had that cinema can help understand moments we’re living in – particularly political moments or moments of crisis, moments of violence, moments of extreme state abuse of power,” said Poitras, who has returned to these themes often in her films on fellow chroniclers Edward Snowden , Julian Assange and the investigative journalist Seymour Hersh . “We have these tools that can get at truth in different types of ways that are emotional.”

And even though the DHS’s recent change in tactics, from shock-and-awe to blending into the background and lying in wait , would seem to suggest that the federal government’s offensive has only evolved, the fact that it was even forced to turn down the temperature gives this horror story satisfying heroes: Minnesota residents who were clearly underestimated as hapless victims. “There’s a history of resistance here that goes back decades,” Mueller said. “Early labor movements started here. The American Indian movement started in the Twin Cities. The resistance that happened in Minneapolis would not have been possible if the networks weren’t in place after the uprising after George Floyd ’s murder. And that uprising wouldn’t have happened if Philando Castile hadn’t been killed. Each one of these pieces builds upon itself.”

articles.title: How AI could ‘supercharge’ election risks across south-east Asia
articles.summary: Some experts fear AI could be weaponised in south-east Asia, home to nations with predominately young and hyper-connected populations Years ago it would have been an elaborate operation involving an army of cyber troops creating fake news websites, social media accounts and forged dossiers, all deployed to spread disinformation en masse. Now, all you need is AI. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Some experts fear AI could be weaponised in south-east Asia, home to nations with predominately young and hyper-connected populations

Y ears ago it would have been an elaborate operation involving an army of cyber troops creating fake news websites, social media accounts and forged dossiers, all deployed to spread disinformation en masse.

In a worrying sign of how AI could “supercharge” fake news, Anthropic recently revealed how Claude AI was used in a political influence operation in Malaysia. It created a commercial election manipulation platform, utilising a network of about 1,000 X accounts, a fake news outlet called “Malaysia Pulse” and a series of fabricated documents.

The operation appeared designed to target voters in recent state elections, pulling in census and electoral data to exploit sensitive political and social fractures, including race, religion, and royalty across all 222 Malaysian parliamentary constituencies.

The experiment was ultimately ineffective once Anthropic stepped in but has sparked alarm about how AI could be weaponised in future elections in south-east Asia, a region already deeply vulnerable to fake news.

Katie Harbath, who formerly worked on public policy for global elections at Meta, says the case is an example of how AI brings a new level of sophistication and ease to the disinformation landscape.

“AI can supercharge it in terms of you can make a lot more content that’s more personalised, quicker and cheaper,” says Harbath, who now heads the tech consultancy company Anchor Change. “But you still need a distribution mechanism, and at the moment, that’s still your more social media type platforms.”

Anthropic detailed the Malaysia election operation in its latest threat assessment, released in September . The report revealed how actors used Claude to build networks of fake social media profiles and news websites that targeted audiences on six continents. Anthropic said the actors included “governments, state-aligned propaganda institutions and state media, as well as private firms selling influence”.

South-east Asia is no stranger to disinformation. In recent years Nobel laureate and Filipino journalist Maria Ressa has likened the Philippines to a “petri dish” for the weaponisation of disinformation and fake news, with techniques tried and tested in the south-east Asian nation later successfully replicated in the west.

“Basically AI is just mimicking what we would have, I guess, termed a few years ago, a troll factory,” says Rossine Fallorina of Sigla, a Philippine thinktank that researches AI. “Mostly because it speeds up the production process. So you don’t need 10 people to create a narrative or a story. You can just prompt it and then have it propagated.”

Last year OpenAI banned accounts using AI to generate comments about Philippine politics and public officials across social platforms, with many fictitious comments generated in support of President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr.

Across south-east Asia, home to nations with predominately young and hyper connected populations, some fear the divisive potential of AI on social media.

“It feeds political polarisation and it feeds on divisions,” says Bridget Welsh, from the University of Nottingham Asia Research Institute Malaysia. “That’s really what’s concerning about the fragmented nature of what’s happening in Malaysia.”

Malaysia’s general election could be called for late 2027, while the Philippines and Cambodia have polls in 2028, and Indonesia the following year.

Already in the region, AI has been effective. In Indonesia, an AI-generated cartoon image of now-president Prabowo Subianto that helped soften his strongman image became wildly popular in the 2024 election.

It has also been used to inflame tensions, such as inciting hatred toward ethnic Rohingya refugees who fled to Malaysia from Myanmar during the civil war, says Dr Ben Loh, a media lecturer at Monash University Malaysia.

“It’s come to the point where people already have this deep-seated hate in their minds and when they see the content like this, even though it’s AI-generated to them, it’s merely reinforcing what they believe is already true,” says Loh.

The Anthropic report notes that the fake news outlet scraped legitimate Malaysian reporting and had the model rewrite it several times before republishing it under fabricated bylines. It also republished articles from Russian and Chinese state-aligned foreign outlets, including TV BRICS, Xinhua, Sputnik/RIA, and CGTN, stripping them of attribution.

Anthropic said in its threat assessment that in each case of identified political influence the company “disrupted the activity, used what we learned to strengthen our safeguards, and shared intelligence with authorities and industry partners, where appropriate”.

In future, Harbath says AI could be used to “flood the zone” in an attempt to influence the large language models (LLMs) from which AI models draw their information.

“If there’s any sort of news drought, or if you have a place where there’s mostly government-sponsored media,” she says, “It wouldn’t take very much money to kind of flood the zone.”

articles.title: Tiny image sparks big backlash in Nikon photo contest
articles.summary: Dr Ning Xu denies he broke the rules of Nikon's annual Small World In Motion contest.
articles.content:
Watch: The competition's winner and runners up. Nikon is investigating whether the winning video (shown left) was altered with AI

The winning entry of a prestigious scientific photography competition is being re-evaluated following criticism from other scientists that it was made with AI.

Nikon's annual Small World In Motion contest accepts photos and video taken using powerful microscopes, and has run annually for the last 15 years.

The winner was a short video submitted by Dr Ning Xu, a researcher at Tsinghua University in China, which claims to be footage of tiny, hair-like structures called cilia moving inside the airways of a child with a rare disease.

Xu did not respond to the BBC's request for comment, but has posted online denying he broke the competition rules.

In a response to a post by Nikon on LinkedIn , external , he did not dispute using AI within the image processing but said he remained within the rules of the contest.

"AI was not used to generate the experimental movie, the cilia, or their motion," he said.

Xu's video is artificially brightly coloured - common in microscopy and permitted in the contest - which is usually done manually using stains and dyes on the sample itself.

He accepted AI was used "to distinguish and visualize features in the reconstructed grayscale images".

But the challenges made by other scientists include claims that the video contains shapes and movements which did not fit with normal cell structures or behaviours, and that the cilia seemed to be too big.

Commenting on Nikon's social media post, Edward Phelps, associate professor at Florida University, observed some of the structures "pop in and out of existence" and the cilia "appear from nowhere".

Meanwhile PhD student Ian Donovan from UT Southwestern Medical Centre said the source image appeared to contain a distinctive watermark indicating it had been AI generated.

Additionally, two former competition judges said they also had concerns about whether the image was real.

Nikon said Xu was "respectfully complying" with its investigation and had provided it with additional technical documents.

Dr Patrick Hickey, who came fifth in the 2026 Small World contest, said the recognition the award represents means more than the $3,000 (£2,250) prize itself.

"If you spend a lot of your time in a dark room looking down a microscope, it's really nice to be able to show people and to show the public," he said.

"There's an interesting fusion between science and art, and a lot of the images that scientists are making have some very abstract and artistic qualities to them."

Hickey said it would be unfair on other entrants if it turned out the winning video was unfairly altered by AI.

"There's a specific set of rules in the contest, and one of them was quite clearly that you couldn't use generative AI to produce things, and the other was obviously that it has to be taken under a microscope," he said.

So far, Nikon is standing by its procedures but it said there would be an update soon.

"At this time, we don't see that any rules were violated," it said in a statement.

articles.title: ‘12 weeks and SO disgusted by my dog’: what happens when you’re pregnant and can’t stand your pet?
articles.summary: There may be almost no research on pet aversion during and post-pregnancy, but it may not be particularly rare About three weeks into her first pregnancy, Sylvia Luu began to loathe the smell of her border collie mix, Ranger. Luu could hardly be in the same room as Ranger without becoming nauseous. His drool repulsed her, and she found the smell of his fur so disgusting she wore a nose plug all day. Continue reading...
articles.content:
There may be almost no research on pet aversion during and post-pregnancy, but it may not be particularly rare

About three weeks into her first pregnancy, Sylvia Luu began to loathe the smell of her border collie mix, Ranger.

Luu could hardly be in the same room as Ranger without becoming nauseous. His drool repulsed her, and she found the smell of his fur so disgusting she wore a nose plug all day.

“Before pregnancy, I used to smell my dog’s paws a lot,” says Luu. “But during pregnancy, I would throw up if I ever tried that.”

At the time, Luu, 35, and Ranger had enjoyed 12 happy years together. Ranger slept in Luu’s bed. She walked him in all weather, and let him lick her face.

Luu’s doctor said that her nausea was normal and simply advised her to drink more water to avoid dehydration from vomiting, but that didn’t alleviate Luu’s distress. “I was so heartbroken that I couldn’t love my dog as much as I wanted to,” says Luu, whose husband took over pet care duties. She wondered about rehoming Ranger, and was relieved when, upon delivering her firstborn, her aversion vanished.

By the time of her second pregnancy, Luu was diagnosed with hyperemesis gravidarum . The condition is caused by hormonal shifts , much like the more familiar morning sickness. For 1%-3% of pregnant people, these shifts result in extreme nausea and disgust sensitivity that can be triggered by any number of things – in this case, pet odour.

Although the diagnosis was helpful, the changes were a difficult and destabilising addition to an already labile time. Luu now wishes that she had received some emotional support from her medical team, practical tips for coping with her diagnosis or validation of the unsettling shift in her feelings toward Ranger.

But there is almost no research into the specific phenomenon of pet aversion during and post-pregnancy.

“This topic is at an intersection of women’s health being underfunded and human-animal bond work being trivialised,” says Dr Katherine Compitus, director of veterinary social work at New York University’s Silver School of Social Work, who has helped clients experiencing pet aversion.

Yet there are signs that prenatal pet aversion isn’t particularly rare.

A survey of 1,077 women who had been pregnant within the past three years found that 15% of pet-owning respondents experienced aversion to their dog during pregnancy, according to 2025 research from the UK pet insurer ManyPets.

On Reddit, pregnant posters complain about feeling annoyed or repelled by their pets’ noises, smells and behaviours. “I’m a huge animal lover but this pregnancy I hate all of them,” wrote one user . “12 weeks and SO disgusted by my dog,” another admitted .

Perinatal depression, anxiety and OCD may contribute to intense, confusing feelings, and a pet may become an outlet for difficult emotions too risky to direct at a partner or child, Compitus says. She recommends that anyone whose feelings about their pets are becoming distressing or out of proportion speak with a therapist, particularly those who use exposure therapy and cognitive behavioral therapy, as these practices can be particularly useful for working through repulsion, rage and disgust.

Katherine Davidson, a dog trainer based in Montreal, noticed herself becoming irritated with the shedding of her three dogs when she became pregnant. “It had never bothered me before,” she says.

But when her daughter was born, the aggravation spiked – something she attributes to practical hygiene concerns and new-mom burnout. “I started feeling resentful” of the dogs, she says, “and that surprised me, because prior, my dogs were my entire life … they were my babies.”

“My postpartum loathing of [pet cat] Lucky made me wonder whether I might be a late-onset psychopath,” mused an anonymous writer in a controversial 2024 essay in the Cut.

The postpartum period can be a vulnerable time for the human-animal bond, says Dr Shelby McDonald, an human-animal interaction researcher and director of the University of Tennessee, Knoxville’s Center for Veterinary Social Work.

New families with pets face challenges including the safety of their baby around a rambunctious dog, and irritation due to barking, shedding and the click-clack of canine nails. “A family’s capacity to meet an animal’s needs may change substantially,” whether physically, emotionally, practically or financially, she says.

“Research with new parents has documented reductions in time and attention devoted to pets … and, for some people, changes in feelings of closeness to their animals,” says McDonald, who is currently collaborating on a study with the University of Edinburgh involving in-depth interviews with mothers in the UK about their experiences with companion animals during pregnancy and postpartum.

Many mothers describe their relationships to their animals improving with time, according to McDonald’s early research.

“A parent can remain deeply attached to an animal while temporarily having much less capacity to care for or interact with them in the way they did before the baby arrived,” she says.

While not yet complete, McDonald’s work also indicates that a minority of mothers relinquish their pets during the postpartum period, seemingly out of concern for the animal’s welfare and quality of life; clear population-level data is not yet available.

There can be “tremendous shame” associated with relinquishing or rehoming an animal, notes McDonald. Yet it’s important for new parents to notice when normal frustration and caregiver fatigue cross into the territory of abuse or neglect, which McDonald describes as an animal being denied adequate food and water, opportunities for exercise and elimination, a reasonably clean and safe environment, veterinary care or social interaction.

“Recognizing that an animal’s welfare and wellbeing is being compromised and making a thoughtful plan for their care can itself be an act of responsible caregiving,” she says. “The priority should be the wellbeing and safety of both the person and the animal, rather than preserving a particular living arrangement at all costs.”

Compitus suggests getting ahead of this issue by getting help from a friend, relative or petsitter. A reputable shelter or rescue may be able to provide guidance; some may even have safety-net programs designed to offer temporary reprieve to overwhelmed pet owners.

Davidson considered rehoming her pets postpartum, but her dilemma was as existential as it was practical. She’d always been a “big animal person”, she says, and the change was confronting.

“You’re just like: ‘Oh, my God, I just need someone to understand, and to tell me these feelings are normal,” says Davidson. Shame and guilt may also contribute to silence around the topic, says Compitus. “If a mother is feeling this aversion toward her pets, it might call into question their identity as a mother: ‘What kind of mother will I be if I can’t even take care of my pet?’”

For Davidson, who ended up keeping her dogs, the negativity she felt toward her pets passed in a matter of months as the household adjusted to a new routine.

Now, when she works with dog-training clients who have growing families, Davidson tells them it’s not unusual to feel frustration or a lack of love for their animals postpartum, and that it often goes away. She shares strategies that worked for her, such as creating pet-free spaces in her home, using a robot vacuum for shedding, and getting help with duties like dog-walking, vet and grooming appointments, and cleaning.

Today, Davidson has three children under six, and has added a six-month-old puppy to her menagerie. “It’s nice having my animals with me, and seeing them grow up with my children,” she says.

She recommends that anyone whose feelings about their pets are becoming distressing or out of proportion speak with a therapist, particularly those who use exposure therapy and cognitive behavioral therapy, as these practices can be particularly useful for working through repulsion, rage and disgust.
Katherine Davidson, a dog trainer based in Montreal, noticed herself becoming irritated with the shedding of her three dogs when she became pregnant. “It had never bothered me before,” she says.

But when her daughter was born, the aggravation spiked – something she attributes to practical hygiene concerns and new-mom burnout. “I started feeling resentful” of the dogs, she says, “and that surprised me, because prior, my dogs were my entire life … they were my babies.”
“My postpartum loathing of [pet cat] Lucky made me wonder whether I might be a late-onset psychopath,” mused an anonymous writer in a controversial 2024 essay in the Cut.

The postpartum period can be a vulnerable time for the human-animal bond, says Dr Shelby McDonald, an human-animal interaction researcher and director of the University of Tennessee, Knoxville’s Center for Veterinary Social Work.

New families with pets face challenges including the safety of their baby around a rambunctious dog, and irritation due to barking, shedding and the click-clack of canine nails. “A family’s capacity to meet an animal’s needs may change substantially,” whether physically, emotionally, practically or financially, she says.

“Research with new parents has documented reductions in time and attention devoted to pets … and, for some people, changes in feelings of closeness to their animals,” says McDonald, who is currently collaborating on a study with the University of Edinburgh involving in-depth interviews with mothers in the UK about their experiences with companion animals during pregnancy and postpartum.
Many mothers describe their relationships to their animals improving with time, according to McDonald’s early research.
“A parent can remain deeply attached to an animal while temporarily having much less capacity to care for or interact with them in the way they did before the baby arrived,” she says.

While not yet complete, McDonald’s work also indicates that a minority of mothers relinquish their pets during the postpartum period, seemingly out of concern for the animal’s welfare and quality of life; clear population-level data is not yet available.

There can be “tremendous shame” associated with relinquishing or rehoming an animal, notes McDonald. Yet it’s important for new parents to notice when normal frustration and caregiver fatigue cross into the territory of abuse or neglect, which McDonald describes as an animal being denied adequate food and water, opportunities for exercise and elimination, a reasonably clean and safe environment, veterinary care or social interaction.

“Recognizing that an animal’s welfare and wellbeing is being compromised and making a thoughtful plan for their care can itself be an act of responsible caregiving,” she says. “The priority should be the wellbeing and safety of both the person and the animal, rather than preserving a particular living arrangement at all costs.”

Compitus suggests getting ahead of this issue by getting help from a friend, relative or petsitter. A reputable shelter or rescue may be able to provide guidance; some may even have safety-net programs designed to offer temporary reprieve to overwhelmed pet owners.
Davidson considered rehoming her pets postpartum, but her dilemma was as existential as it was practical. She’d always been a “big animal person”, she says, and the change was confronting.

“You’re just like: ‘Oh, my God, I just need someone to understand, and to tell me these feelings are normal,” says Davidson. Shame and guilt may also contribute to silence around the topic, says Compitus. “If a mother is feeling this aversion toward her pets, it might call into question their identity as a mother: ‘What kind of mother will I be if I can’t even take care of my pet?’”
For Davidson, who ended up keeping her dogs, the negativity she felt toward her pets passed in a matter of months as the household adjusted to a new routine.

Now, when she works with dog-training clients who have growing families, Davidson tells them it’s not unusual to feel frustration or a lack of love for their animals postpartum, and that it often goes away. She shares strategies that worked for her, such as creating pet-free spaces in her home, using a robot vacuum for shedding, and getting help with duties like dog-walking, vet and grooming appointments, and cleaning.
Today, Davidson has three children under six, and has added a six-month-old puppy to her menagerie. “It’s nice having my animals with me, and seeing them grow up with my children,” she says.

articles.content:
At the start of the competition, it didn’t look like a 1-0 win and two one-goal defeats would be enough for Scotland, but now, that seems likely to qualify them. However, Brazil looked much better in their second game than their first – admittedly against far worse opposition, but it did also look like Carlo Ancelotti is clover to finding his best team. Against Morocco, I was shocked to see Igor Thiago selected ahead of Matheus Cunha; I think we can safely say that will not happen again.

Which I guess brings us to our next round of action. Before we properly dig in, let’s acquaint ourselves with the panoply of permutations.

Colombia played pretty well, I thought, and would’ve won by more were it not for Lionel Mpasi in the DRC net. I was disappointed by the winner because on first look, I thought Daniel Muñoz had done him with the eyes, but it turned out to be a deflection.

Panama have come on loads since England clattered them in 2018 – Ghana also got away with it against them. Luka Modric, though, what a player.

Qatar’s manager, Julen Lopetegui, has revealed Assim Madibo spent the eve of their final Group A match visiting Ismael Kone after the Canada midfielder underwent successful surgery for a broken leg.

Madibo was sent off after inadvertently injuring Kone in last week’s 6-0 defeat to Canada. At the time Madibo was visibly distraught and he has since visited Kone in Vancouver, Canada’s base for the tournament. Kone, who plays in Serie A for Sassuolo, is expected to miss at least five months of action. “It has been very tough for him,” Lopetegui said of Madibo on Tuesday afternoon. “We wish him [Kone] all the best to recover as soon as possible. “Now in the current moment Madibo is in Vancouver visiting Kone because he was very, very affected by this injury – it was never his intention. It was a very clear accident. We wish him all the best.” Madibo is suspended for Qatar’s match against Bosnia and Herzegovina in Seattle on Wednesday. Homam Ahmed is also suspended after being sent off in the same game last Thursday.

Iran prepared for their final Group G match by highlighting the US’s deadly attack on a school that killed at least 168 people, predominantly schoolchildren. Iran’s players trained at their base in Tijuana, Mexico, on Tuesday evening with black corner flags adorned with the message: “#168” . The number refers to the victims who were killed in a strike on an elementary school in Minab, southern Iran, on 28 February, the first day of the US-Israel war on Iran. The attack was attributed to the US military, with Donald Trump last week saying: “Nobody did that on purpose. Mistakes are made. The war is nasty.” When Iran first landed at their base in Mexico earlier this month, after a training camp in Turkey, they arrived wearing pin badges on their lapels that read: “#168”. Iran will arrive in Seattle from Tijuana at 11.30am local time on Wednesday before facing Egypt on Friday after being granted special permission to arrive in the US two days before the game. The match is the World Cup’s designated Pride Match, despite both teams complaining to Fifa about the celebrations which will coincide with Seattle’s Pride weekend. After Sunday’s draw with Belgium, Iran left a handwritten note in the dressing room at Los Angeles Stadium in which they called for peace. The message, which also featured #168, read: ““From the ancient Persia of thousands of years ago to the civilised Iran of today, the spirit of Iran remains alive and steadfast. We came to Los Angeles with pride, competed with honour, and leave with dignity “Thank you Los Angeles for your hospitality. And thank you to every Iranian who gave their heart, voice and soul for Iran throughout these 180 minutes. May peace, respect and friendship prevail among all nations.”

Fifa’s view of Iran training with #168 flags remains to be seen. Their regulations state that “equipment must not have any political, religious or personal slogans, statements or images” or players and/or the team may be sanctioned by the competition organiser.

Iran were only permitted to arrive in LA before draws against New Zealand and Belgium 24 hours before the games, leading their head coach, Amir Ghalenoei to label Iran the “most oppressed” team at the tournament.

Also at training on Tuesday, the former Brighton winger Alireza Jahanbakshsh was given a commemorative Iran shirt after reaching 100 caps for his country against Belgium. Fifa has been contacted for comment.

I don’t want to get all conspiracist, but you don’t have be John Le Carré to wonder if TV companies benefitting from ad revenue has an upside for Fifa even though they’re not cut in on each specific deal.

FIFA president Gianni Infantino has defended the introduction of hydration breaks at the World Cup , insisting that for football’s ⁠governing body they are driven purely by sporting considerations and not commercial interests.

This has fuelled debate over their impact on the game, with some viewers complaining about ⁠being exposed to commercials during the three-minute stoppages.

“There is no additional revenue for Fifa, as all ​commercial agreements were signed well in advance. ‌So, this is not ‌a financial issue for us. For us, it is purely a sporting matter,” Infantino said in ‌a statement on Wednesday.

The breaks allow coaching staff to give in-game tactical instructions, a shift critics say disrupts match momentum and fundamentally alters the nature of the game.

England manager Thomas Tuchel said the additional break “interrupts and changes the identity of the football match“, while Uruguay coach Marcelo Bielsa said dividing matches into shorter segments takes away the fundamental characteristic ‌of the game.

Spain coach Luis de la Fuente and Netherlands captain Virgil van Dijk have supported the intent behind the rule in extreme heat, but questioned ​the need for it in cooler conditions and at covered venues.

“The main reason is the heat, but we also have to understand that in a competition like the (FIFA) World Cup, played over 39 days, with teams potentially playing eight matches in those 39 days, having a moment to rest ⁠is extremely important,” Infantino said.

“What matters even more to us is ensuring ​that all teams, in every ​match, are playing under the ​same conditions.

“It’s very difficult to accept that a coach might have the opportunity ​to influence a ‌match by making adjustments ​simply because it’s ​hotter, while in another match, where the temperature is slightly lower, the same coach doesn’t have the same opportunity.”

Infantino added that the breaks had not reduced the intensity of matches, suggesting players were able to maintain a high level of performance throughout games.

“Is it possible we all got over excited by England beating an old and possibly quite poor Croatia team (who laboured to a 1-0 win over Panama)?” wonders Samuel Dodson. “Tuchel’s record against any reasonable side seems to be losses against Japan and Senegal and a draw against another ailing once-decent side in Uruguay. Friendlies don’t really matter, of course; and that second half surge for 15 minutes really was very fun. And not very much like how we expect England to play. This stodgy draw against Ghana however is exactly how I expect England to play. Remember 0-0 against Algeria? The USA? The good news of course is that the performance and result means we can go back to what we do best – endless debate and faux controversy and anger over team selections. Had we beaten Ghana comfortably here in not sure we or the media would have quite known how to react or what to talk about.”

Croatia definitely played into England’s hands, but the way they took control of the game was impressive. Watching it, my sense was that at some point, the defence would let them down, and Japan are a particularly difficult opponent for how they’re trying to play – so too Spain – but on a good day they can beat anyone and even on a bad day, they’ve the attacking talent to save themselves. Do I think they’re likely champions? No, but I don’t think it’s impossible.

Remember 2018, when Emmanuel Macron got drenched as Vladimir Putin relaxed under an umbrella held for him? How will Trump assert himself to this level?

I was really disappointed with Reece James. He’s a superb player capable of so much better going forward and England really needed that from him – overlaps, underlaps and crosses. But he delivered almost nothing.

Email! “‘I don’t care about Messi’ was such an insulting and insensitive remark from such a talented player,” says Krishnamoorthy V of Ronaldo. “This is what ego does to your personality. Ghana sending CR7 and co home will be so satisfying.”

I think that imperviousness has made Ronaldo what he is. Of course, he’s not really impervious at all, but thinks he is, and that’s all that matters.

Jacob makes a fair point here, that Palmer and Foden didn’t do enough to force their way into the squad. But both are special talents who’ve shown quality miles beyond that which we’ve seen from Madueke and Gordon, who are not, and neither of whom were all that good last season either.

Again, though, I come back to the big-space/small-space thing, and the lack of balance in the squad. And, judging by the substitutions, it’s not something management see as an issue – the changes were like for like, rather than seeking to alter or vary the method of attack.

The good news for England is that, as they progress, teams will, most likely, look to attack them, leaving space for their speed and physicality to exploit. But the squad lack guile and magic, completely unnecessarily, and it’s not clear Tuchel really groks that.

Anderson, Rice and Bellingham are all fantastic players, but none have the deftness around the box to play quick combinations, or the eye to thread through little passes. It was obvious at half-time that, given what was available, the wise move was to hook one of the first two for Kobbie Mainoo, who is brilliant at finding space in traffic.

Or, in other words, a balanced midfield is not three power-players; at least one touch-player is required, and Mainoo is the only one England have. Perhaps you might say Eberechi Eze is that too, and he came on far too late to influence the game or for it to look like the coaching staff are on top of the problem.

I agree with Barney here: this was a small-space game, in which England used big-space players.

Partly this is because of the squad Thomas Tuchel picked. If I was facing England and you offered me Noni Madueke, Cole Palmer and Phil Foden, I know which of those three I’d back myself against. Madueke is a decent player, but no more than that; he isn’t special, and the other two are.

Palmer, in particular, has the ability to change the pace of a game and do surprising things others can’t, exactly what you need against an organised low block. But that wast the only glaring issue: Lewis Hall would’ve given England natural width on the left and also excellent passing out of defence, but he’s not even in the squad; and, though Trent Alexander-Arnold is no one’s idea of a proper defender, if you’re using him it’s because you need a goal, and leaving his delivery and craft at home makes absolutely no sense.

I wonder if these errors reflect a manager unfamiliar with tournament football; Tuchel has decided to play a particular way, and picked a collection of profiles he thinks can do that. But that’s left him without the means to change things properly; if things go wrong, he can swap players, but what if, as yesterday, the issue is the system and its principles?

And was Jordan Pickford fortunate not to get a red card when he hared out of box to collide with Abdul Fatawu?

I feel not. Had Fatawu got a touch on the ball, Pickford was toast, but because neither player did, I don’t think we can say there was a foul. Both went for it, both missed, so it makes most sense is to call it a collision.

I don’t really see how you can’t give it. Fatawu was in and Konsa launches into him, getting nowhere near the ball with no chance of getting at the ball – which makes it a red card too.

As far as goalless draws go, I thought it an engaging one. But plenty of things for Thomas Tuchel to ponder, which we’ll dig into into which we’ll dig presently.

This “I’m back” situation, though; it’ll take more than bagging a brace against Uzbekistan for that to be so.

Roberto Martínez has options, too. He could play a wide player up front – Pedro Neto has done it for Chelsea – or Goncalo Ramos, who’s a striker.

But it’s not just Ronaldo preventing this team from working as it should – Bernardo Silva was left out and, if they’re to fulfil their potential – they’ve got the players to win the thing – he must surely play a key role. I’d get him into a midfield three with Vitinha and João Neves, then have Bruno Fernandes and Neto with free roles behind – if we must – Ronaldo.

Surely no one rhose surname isn’t Dos Santos Aveiro really thinks that, though? Ronaldo can still finish – he’ll never lose that – but it’s very hard to even come up with rationale, never mind believe rationale, that says the best version of this Portugal team contains him.

We go again! We’ll begin by reflecting on the latest action – Portugal getting their competition going by thrashing Uzbekistan, England and Ghana near-enough securing passage to the knockouts, Croatia just about seeing off Panama, now eliminated, and Colombia forcing their way past DR Congo.

Then, when we’ve done that, we’ll build up to today’s action, featuring the final round of matches in Group B – Switzerland v Canada and Bosnia and Herzegovina v Qatar; Group C – Morocco v Haiti and Scotland v Brazil… and Group A – South Africa v South Korea and Czechia v México.

I reckon some people might have some thoughts about all of that lot, so we’ll share those of our writers, but do send in yours too.

articles.content:
Alex Freeman has impressed from right-back while Eli Just is catching the eye with his body swerves and goal threat

It is not difficult to see why this old head on young shoulders is destined for a big career. In a Morocco team conditioned to play first-time passes, he sets the tone with his instant decisions. Bouaddi is in essence the deepest of the midfield three and he not only plays quickly but often finds a colleague in a more forward position. Strong on the ball, he can intercept from his central position and looks to continue his involvement after playing a pass. Bouaddi can tackle and shield a ball and finds space naturally. With his height, at 6ft 1in, technique and football intelligence, he will not be a Lille player for much longer. When Bouaddi gets forward he should try to be more positive – to be a more complete player he will need to have a few goals on his CV – but he is a real talent.

Mauricio Pochettino has made a dream World Cup start with the USA. All his players have performed with pace and positivity, limiting opponents to few opportunities, and Freeman, the youngest in his squad, has caught my eye with his contributions from right-back. When a poor Australia side threatened, he made a superb last-ditch challenge, intercepting a low cross. Previously I had noticed a player cool in possession who keeps the play moving with an early pass rather a big kick upfield. Freeman left Orlando for the Spanish overachievers Villarreal in January and shows maturity beyond his years. He is also brave and, not long after a heavy clash of heads, he leaped to score the USA’s second goal against Australia . At close quarters when confronted he showed a sharp change of feet to escape an attacker and he can tackle too and has enough pace.

Playing as the left centre-back in a four-man defence, he has impressed alongside three more experienced defenders. The 6ft 4in player is in line to play a second season in Serie A with Sassuolo after the tournament, having been a major contributor to their 2025 promotion while on loan from Juventus. I would compare him to Luka Vuskovic, the Croatian who joined Tottenham last summer and went on loan to Hamburg. Muharemovic is not as aggressive in the air but wins his share of headers and I like his calm play under pressure, making interceptions, anticipating danger and reading the game. When passing he always looks to play forward – breaking the lines in today’s parlance – and his passing accuracy is high. He is also forceful when moving with the ball and always aware of his distance to fellow defenders. Against Switzerland he was sent off for a last-ditch challenge to prevent a goal in the 80th minute and the opposition took full advantage, scoring a further three times, but as he walked off he could hold his head high.

His World Cup performances have captured a wider audience than he had last season in Scotland, where he delighted supporters of an improving Motherwell side with consistently high-quality displays. An intelligent middle-to-front forward, Just is a late developer. He previously played in Denmark and Austria after leaving New Zealand and is now showing a belief in his ability. Bigger defenders have been caught off balance by a quick body swerve as he moves with intent from the middle third into dangerous areas and at this tournament he has benefited from complementing the strength and hold-up play of Chris Wood. Just’s advantage over similar attacking midfielders is how quick he is to assess situations – he sees pictures. Twice against Iran he saw the space in which to receive from his target man and score with perfectly placed right-foot shots. He can score with his left too but needs to score more. Just is consistently a highly skilled performer at club level and shows a commendable humbleness and intelligence. If he continues his improvement he will be on a bigger club’s radar.

The introduction of the forward in the last minutes of the game against Bosnia and Herzegovina was quite dramatic. Within minutes this powerful, speedy, right-footed player destroyed his opponents’ hopes of surviving with a draw. They had just lost Muharemovic and Manzambi exploited the extra space with perfect timing to get two goals. When he scored the first, a well taken volley, it was clear he would be the centre of attention and it reminded me of the impact on Michael Owen’s life when he brushed past Argentina defenders to score for England in Saint-Étienne. Manzambi spent his early days with Servette before moving to Freiburg and has shown he has the pace and power, combined with adequate control, to trouble defenders in the Bundesliga. He seems well respected by his colleagues there but after contributing a combined 16 goals and assists for his club this season, he may soon have new teammates.

articles.title: US to probe petrol price gouging claims, Trump says
articles.summary: The president's remarks come as global oil prices have fallen but remain higher than before the US-Israel war with Iran.
articles.content:
US President Donald Trump has said he has ordered an investigation into major energy companies, accusing them of "gouging" customers by not cutting petrol prices after wholesale oil costs fell on global markets.

Trump wrote on social media that he has ordered the Department of Justice (DOJ) to "immediately start looking into this", adding he had expected to see petrol prices fall "a lot faster than what I'm seeing." He did not name any oil firms in the post.

His remarks come after the price of oil fell from peaks seen during the US-Israel war with Iran but remain higher than before the conflict started.

"The big Oil Companies are not dropping their price at the pump commensurate with the sharply lower prices they are paying for Oil," Trump said in the post.

"Those prices are dropping like a rock! In other words, customers are being 'gouged.'"

Oil prices shot up after Iran responded to US-Israeli strikes on 28 February by effectively shutting the critical Strait of Hormuz waterway , severely disrupting shipments of oil and gas and causing energy prices to soar.

Brent crude, the global wholesale oil benchmark, reached almost $120 (£91) a barrel in May as the war continued.

But prices have fallen since as peace talks have progressed. On Wednesday, Brent dropped below $76 a barrel, but it is still above the roughly $70 a barrel mark it was at before the conflict.

It is a similar picture with the US wholesale oil benchmark, WTI crude, which dipped under $72 a barrel on Wednesday but remains higher than before the war when it traded at around $60 a barrel.

Meanwhile, the average price of regular gasoline in the US has fallen to about $3.93 a gallon after topping $4 a gallon in April , its highest since 2022, but is still well above pre-war levels.

Trump's comments come after UK oil firms faced similar accusations of unfairly hiking petrol prices following the start of the Iran war.

However, the UK competition regulator said in May there was no widespread evidence of this , adding that average profit margins were "broadly unchanged" between February and March.

articles.title: France braces for another day of sweltering heat as Europe heatwave spreads
articles.summary: The heatwave is expected to spread to other parts of western Europe on Wednesday, before extending eastwards over the weekend.
articles.content:
France is bracing for another day of exceptionally hot weather, with more than half the country remaining under a red heat alert on Wednesday.

Tens of thousands of homes have been left without power in western Brittany, while a major wildfire was brought under control overnight in the Maine-et-Loire region.

It comes after the country experienced its hottest June day since records began on Tuesday, with an average temperature of 29.8C (85.54F) recorded.

The heatwave is expected to spread to other parts of western Europe on Wednesday, with an orange alert for dangerous weather in place for parts of the Netherlands.

Temperatures are expected to peak in the Netherlands and Belgium on Friday, while Germany is expected to see the mercury rise to 40C (104F) over the weekend.

The heatwave is also expected to spread to eastern Europe over the next few days, with severe heat warnings issued for countries including Poland, Croatia and Hungary for later in the week.

So far, France, Spain and Italy have been hardest hit by the heatwave.

Forty people have drowned in heatwave-related incidents in France since last Thursday, according to the prime minister.

Red alerts in France are being extended to include four more regions as of midday on Wednesday, forecaster Météo France said, bringing the total number to 58. Thirty-one more regions are under an orange alert.

UK braces for extreme heat as Met Office warns of health risks and transport delays

The top temperatures forecast across Europe on Wednesday - with France expected to see the hottest conditions

As of 05:00 local time, La Rochelle in the southwest had already recorded a temperature of 29C, the forecaster said, with a high of 43C possible later in the day in the region.

Highs of 39 to 40C are forecast across much of the country's west, from Paris to Brittany, and are expected to remain the same until the weekend.

Temperatures peaked on Tuesday, with a high of 44.3C recorded in parts of Landes, in the southwest.

Some relief from the heat is expected from Friday, with temperatures forecast to gradually drop over the weekend. This change will come with thunderstorms, bringing a risk of flash flooding and large hail.

Speaking to French radio, labour minister Jean-Pierre Farandou said "we're in the process of finding out we've become a hot country".

The heat caused the first major power outage in the country, with around 68,000 homes left without power in the north-western Finistère region on Tuesday evening due to a problem with a transformer, authorities said. Power is not expected to be restored for everyone until the end of Wednesday at the earliest.

Elsewhere in the Maine and Loire region, more than 150 firefighters were deployed to fight a major fire on Tuesday in the Breignon forest in Saint-Macaire-du-Bois. It was brought under control overnight, authorities said.

Sights in the French capital Paris have also been impacted by the hot weather.

The world's most visited museum, the Louvre, said it was bringing forward its closing time from Wednesday to Saturday from 18:00 to 16:00 local time.

The Louvre said its historic building "remains fragile, external and is not sufficiently adapted to climate change", adding that the "build-up of heat is at its highest at the end of the day, and intensified by the volume of visitors".

In France, among those who died in heatwave-related incidents was a 13-year-old girl who had gone for a dip with her family in the River Seine at Fontaine-La Port on Sunday evening, although she did not know how to swim.

From cool-down spots to chalk on windows - how Europe is coping with the heat

Red heat alerts issued in France, Italy and Spain as 40C temperatures forecast

While Spain has experienced baking heat over the last few days, temperatures are expected to start falling on the Iberian peninsula on Wednesday.

But red heat alerts remain in place for parts of northern Spain, with a maximum temperature of 42C possible in parts of the Basque country, forecaster Aemet said.

In Italy, meanwhile, 16 provincial capitals are now under red heat alerts, with Latina added to the list on Wednesday, while Bari will be added on Thursday, Italian news agency Ansa said.

The Dutch weather service, the KNMI, has issued a Code Orange weather alert, which refers to a "high chance of dangerous weather" in southern and central areas of the Netherlands from Wednesday until at least Friday.

KNMI said maximum temperatures of 37C were expected, while Friday could see the mercury hit 39C.

In Belgium, most of the country is under an orange alert with highs of 37C expected over the next few days.

After meeting on Tuesday, Belgium's Risk Management Group said it was activating the "alert phase of the national ozone and heat plan" for only the second time. The first occasion was in August 2020, although no specific national measures have been announced, other than to raise awareness and call for extra care for the elderly and children.

Climate change is driving up temperatures around the world - but particularly in Europe. It is the fastest warming continent, heating up twice as fast as the global average, according to the Copernicus climate service , external .

This is causing increased summer heatwaves, greater pressure on Europe's water supply, and more intense wildfires. Last year, more than one million hectares burnt across Europe - a record level - with Spain particularly affected.

articles.title: Burnham likely to replace Reeves if he becomes PM
articles.summary: Rachel Reeves would be offered a more junior cabinet role, the BBC understands.
articles.content:
Andy Burnham is expected to replace Rachel Reeves as chancellor and offer her a more junior cabinet position if he becomes prime minister, the BBC understands.

A spokesperson for Burnham said no decisions had been made about who he would appoint.

The MP for Makerfield is the only candidate to have emerged so far for the Labour leadership, and has met Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer for talks as he prepares for a likely entry to No 10.

Senior Cabinet minister Darren Jones ruled himself out of the running for the leadership on Wednesday, and if there are no other candidates, Burnham could become prime minister by 17 July.

The biggest decision Burnham will make as he begins to sketch out a possible cabinet is who will be his chancellor, and most Labour MPs assume Reeves will not continue in that role.

As first reported by the Financial Times , external , she is expected to be offered a more junior cabinet position.

A close ally of Burnham told the BBC: "Andy really respects Rachel and I'm confident he'll want her in his top team."

It is unclear who might replace Reeves as chancellor, with Ed Miliband, Wes Streeting, John Healey and Yvette Cooper among the names mooted.

James Purnell, who served as a minister in Gordon Brown's government between 2007 and 2009, is expected to become Burnham's Downing Street chief of staff.

Burnham's people: MPs and advisers in line for a job if he gains power

Paul Johnson, former director if the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said any chancellor had a number of difficult decisions to take.

He said the UK had borrowed more than virtually any other country in the last 25 years at very high rates, but had also failed to grow to pay off the debt.

"Simply borrowing more is certainly not an easy thing to do and it's absolutely not a costless thing to do," he told BBC Radio 4's Today programme, adding: "Growth clearly is the number one priority."

He said: "That requires a lot of really quite difficult decisions in terms of not just increasing taxes but reforming taxes, reforming welfare, focusing investment on the things that are actually likely to get you growth, radically changing regulatory and planning regimes.

"All of those sorts of things, and that's something where I think we need a really clear indication from a new chancellor that they're really focused on."

Another immediate challenges for a new prime minister is how much to spend on defence, following the row over the controversial defence spending proposals, which triggered the resignations of two defence ministers.

Burnham and his team have been discussing that with John Healey, the former defence secretary, warning the current planned increase in military funding fell "well short of what is required".

Sir Keir met Burnham for an hour on Tuesday, as the outgoing leader sought to ensure an "orderly" transition of power.

articles.title: Kenya to charge students with murder over deadly school fire
articles.summary: Sixteen pupils, aged between 15 and 18, died when a fire broke out in a dormitory at Utumishi Girls' School last month.
articles.content:
Eight students are still in police custody following their arrest last month

Kenyan prosecutors say they are preparing to charge several students with the murder of their schoolmates following a suspected school arson attack last month.

Sixteen pupils, aged between 15 and 18, died and dozens more were injured when a fire broke out in a dormitory at Utumishi Girls' School in Gilgil, about 120km (77 miles) north-west of the capital, Nairobi.

Eight students were later arrested after police said they may have been involved in starting the fire by setting mattresses alight near an exit.

"Upon careful assessment of the evidence, the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) has approved charges against the implicated students," the state prosecutor's office said in a statement.

The 28 May fire tore through the upper floor of a dormitory containing 135 bunk beds and housing 202 students, forcing them to flee through a single doorway after the emergency exit failed to open.

After interviews with students and staff and a forensic review of CCTV footage, eight pupils at the school were identified as "persons of interest in connection with the planning and execution" of the fire," police said.

The suspects, who are being held in custody, are due to be formally charged in court, following a review of evidence gathered by investigators.

"The suspects will face sixteen (16) counts of murder arising from the incident," the said the Office of the DPP.

Prosecutors did not say how many suspects would be charged or when the charges would be brought in court. The students are expected to appear in court in Naivasha on Wednesday.

The ODPP has expressed concern over a recent rise in cases of arson and related criminal conduct in learning institutions across the country, warning that those responsible would be held accountable.

Education Minister Julius Ogamba said preliminary findings indicated that there had been multiple breaches of safety measures at Utumishi Girls' School, including overcrowding in dormitories and a locked exit door.

Kenya has a long history of school fires - just two years ago at least 21 people died in a dormitory fire in central Kenya.

Many fires reported in boarding schools have been the result of arson, with disgruntled pupils - angry about disciplinary measures and living conditions - accused of being responsible, while others were caused by accident.

Overcrowding in dormitories and the failure to follow safety guidelines, such as keeping exits clear and windows unlocked, have frequently been blamed for the high number of casualties.
